domains.name: Kotlin Core
domains.summary: Null safety, data/sealed classes, the coroutines mental model, extension functions, and delegation — the language half of every Android loop.

scenarios.title: The billion-dollar mistake
scenarios.situation: Kotlin round. The interviewer shows `val name: String? = intent.getStringExtra("name")` and asks you to greet the user.
scenarios.prompt: Which is the idiomatic null-safe approach?
choices: `val greeting = name?.let { "Hello, $it" } ?: "Hello, guest"` — safe call plus Elvis covers null without ever asserting non-null.
`"Hello, ${name!!}"` — the extra is always present, so assert it.
`if (name != null) "Hello, $name" else "Hello, guest"` then cast name with `as String` — explicit is better.
Declare the parameter as `String!` (platform type) and ignore nullability — Java interop handles it.
scenarios.why: Kotlin's type system tracks nullability: `String?` vs `String`. Safe call `?.`, Elvis `?:`, and `let` handle nulls explicitly; `!!` throws NPE on null and is the thing interviewers want you to avoid. Platform types from Java (`String!`) are the interop hazard — the compiler cannot help you there.
scenarios.hint: Which operator lets you act on the value only when it is non-null, and what provides the fallback?

scenarios.title: Data class or plain class?
scenarios.situation: Kotlin round. You model API responses: `User(id, name, email)` compared, copied, and logged.
scenarios.prompt: Why is a data class the right call, and what does it give you?
choices: `data class` generates equals/hashCode, toString, copy(), and componentN destructuring — value-like semantics for models; a plain class gives you identity equality and boilerplate you would hand-write.
Data classes are faster at runtime — the compiler optimizes their allocation.
Plain classes are required for JSON parsing; data classes cannot be deserialized.
They are identical; `data` is just documentation.
scenarios.why: Data classes are Kotlin's answer to model boilerplate: structural equality means two Users with the same fields are equal (what you want for DiffUtil and tests), copy() gives cheap immutable updates, and destructuring works in when-branches. Caveats worth naming: data classes should stay simple (no heavy logic), and inheritance from them is restricted.
scenarios.hint: What breaks in a RecyclerView diff if equality is identity-based instead of structural?
objectives: Choose data classes for model types

scenarios.title: Sealed class for UI state
scenarios.situation: Architecture round. A screen can be Loading, Content(items), or Error(message). The interviewer bans booleans like `isLoading`.
choices: `sealed interface UiState { data object Loading : UiState; data class Content(val items: List<Item>) : UiState; data class Error(val msg: String) : UiState }` — the compiler enforces exhaustive `when`, so adding a state breaks the build until every branch handles it.
Three booleans: isLoading, hasError, isEmpty — simple and readable.
An enum with three constants — states never carry data anyway.
A String field holding "loading"/"content"/"error" — flexible for future states.
scenarios.why: Sealed hierarchies make illegal states unrepresentable: you cannot be Loading and Error at once, unlike three booleans (8 combinations, most invalid). Exhaustive when is the payoff — the compiler becomes your reviewer when states evolve. This is the standard UDF UiState pattern on Android.
scenarios.hint: How many invalid combinations do three booleans allow, and who catches them?
objectives: Model UI state as sealed hierarchies

scenarios.title: Extension function vs member
scenarios.situation: Kotlin round. You need `String.isValidEmail()` used across the app. The interviewer asks where it should live.
scenarios.prompt: What is the right design, and what is the key limitation to name?
choices: An extension function in a shared util file: it reads like a member, needs no subclassing — but extensions are resolved statically, so they cannot be overridden and cannot access private members; if polymorphism is needed, use a real member or interface.
A member function on String — subclass String and add it.
A static utility class with `StringUtils.isValidEmail(s)` — extensions are syntactic sugar with hidden costs.
An extension property with a backing field — extensions can hold state.
scenarios.why: Extensions are static dispatch: the function called depends on the compile-time type, not the runtime type — the classic interview trap is expecting virtual dispatch. They also cannot see privates or add state. The power: extending final classes and platform types without wrappers.
scenarios.hint: If you 'override' an extension in a subclass, which one runs — and why does that surprise people?

scenarios.title: Delegation in one keyword
scenarios.situation: Whiteboard round. 'Implement an observable property: log every assignment, without repeating code in each setter.'
scenarios.prompt: What is the idiomatic Kotlin solution?
choices: Property delegation: `var name: String by Delegates.observable("<none>") { _, old, new -> log("$old -> $new") }` — or a custom `ReadWriteProperty` for reusable logic; delegation composes where inheritance would tangle.
A base class with a custom setter that subclasses override — inheritance is the OOP answer.
A global map from property name to listener, updated manually in each setter.
Reflection: scan fields at runtime and intercept writes — fully generic.
scenarios.why: `by` delegates getter/setter to an object implementing getValue/setValue — `lazy`, `observable`, `vetoable` are stdlib examples, and custom delegates encapsulate cross-cutting logic (validation, persistence, logging) once. Class delegation (`class Repo(...) : Api by apiImpl`) does the same for interfaces. Name the mechanism: the compiler generates the forwarding.
scenarios.hint: What code would you otherwise copy into every setter — and what language feature generates it for you?

scenarios.title: Variance: in and out
scenarios.situation: Generics round. You have `Producer<out T>` and `Consumer<in T>`. The interviewer asks why a `Producer<Dog>` is assignable to `Producer<Animal>`.
choices: `out T` declares covariance: T only appears in output positions, so a producer of Dogs is usable wherever a producer of Animals is expected — type-safe because you can only get Animals out. `in T` is contravariance for consumers; invariant `T` allows neither.
Kotlin generics are covariant by default, like Java arrays.
It is assignable because Dog and Animal are both classes — any generic of related types is assignable.
Variance is a runtime check the JVM performs on each call.
scenarios.why: Use-site vs declaration-site variance is a senior filter: `out` (producer) = covariant, `in` (consumer) = contravariant, plain `T` = invariant. The mnemonic is PECS (producer-extends, consumer-super). Star projections (`*`) come up with unknown type arguments. Java's `? extends` is the use-site cousin.
scenarios.hint: If you can only take Ts OUT of it, what harm is there in treating it as a producer of a supertype?

scenarios.title: The Platform Type Trap
scenarios.situation: Your Kotlin code calls a Java library method declared as String getDisplayName(). In production, it occasionally returns null and your app crashes with an NPE on a non-null Kotlin String.
choices: Treat the platform type as hostile: assign to a nullable (String?) or add an explicit null check / Elvis with a fallback at the interop boundary.
Wrap every Java call in try/catch NullPointerException.
Rewrite the Java library in Kotlin.
Declare the result as String (non-null) — the Java signature says String, so trust it.
scenarios.why: The correct approach respects platform types: Java's String compiles to String! — the compiler makes no guarantee. Null-checking or Elvis at the boundary converts uncertainty into an explicit decision. Trusting the signature reintroduces the NPE; try/catch on NPE is exception abuse; rewriting the library is disproportionate.
scenarios.hint: What does the ! in String! mean?
evidence: NPE at greeting.kt:42 — getDisplayName() returned null despite String signature

domains.name: Android Framework
domains.summary: Activities, fragments, lifecycles, intents, views, services, and permissions — the platform mechanics interviewers probe.

scenarios.title: Activity lifecycle order
scenarios.situation: Framework round. 'Walk me through the activity lifecycle when the user gets a phone call mid-form.'
choices: onPause (call UI takes over; save light state) -> onStop (fully obscured) — and on return onRestart -> onStart -> onResume; the form's unsaved input belongs in onSaveInstanceState or a ViewModel, not in onPause file writes.
onDestroy -> onCreate — the system kills and recreates the activity on every interruption.
onStop -> onPause — stop fires before pause when obscured quickly.
Nothing happens — phone calls are handled by the system without touching the activity.
scenarios.why: The order is onCreate -> onStart -> onResume (visible + interactive), then onPause -> onStop (-> onDestroy). onPause must be fast (it blocks the incoming activity); heavy saves go to onStop or background. Configuration changes (rotation) destroy and recreate — which is why ViewModel exists.
scenarios.hint: Which callback must return instantly because it gates the incoming screen — and where does the form data survive rotation?

scenarios.title: Explicit vs implicit intent
scenarios.situation: Framework round. You need to open your own `DetailActivity` with an item id, and separately let the user share text to any app.
scenarios.prompt: Which intent type for each, and why?
choices: Explicit intent (targeting DetailActivity::class.java with the id extra) for in-app navigation — precise and safe; implicit intent (ACTION_SEND with type text/plain and a chooser) for sharing — resolved by the system against installed apps' intent filters.
Implicit for both — the system resolves your own activities too.
Explicit for both — hardcode the share target package for reliability.
Broadcasts for both — intents are legacy; broadcasts are the modern API.
scenarios.why: Explicit = named component (in-app, secure); implicit = action + data resolved via intent filters (cross-app). Extras carry data — Parcelable for custom types. Security note: exported activities receiving implicit intents must validate input; deep links are implicit intents with data URIs.
scenarios.hint: Who resolves each one — your code naming a class, or the system matching filters?
objectives: Choose intent types by trust boundary

scenarios.title: Fragment state loss
scenarios.situation: Framework round. Crash report: `IllegalStateException: Can not perform this action after onSaveInstanceState` from a commit in a network callback.
scenarios.prompt: What is the root cause and the fix?
choices: The transaction commits after the fragment's state was saved (activity backgrounded); the FragmentManager refuses because the state would be lost on restore — fix by committing before state save, using commitAllowingStateLoss only when loss is acceptable, or better, driving navigation from lifecycle-aware state (ViewModel + observer) instead of raw callbacks.
Fragments are deprecated; rewrite with activities to avoid the exception.
Wrap every commit in try/catch — the exception is harmless.
Call `executePendingTransactions()` in the callback — forcing execution bypasses the check.
scenarios.why: The rule: after onSaveInstanceState, the manager has snapshotted state; a commit would diverge from the snapshot. commitAllowingStateLoss silences it but can drop UI state — acceptable for fire-and-forget dialogs, not for navigation. The architectural fix is making commits a function of observed state, which is lifecycle-safe by construction.
scenarios.hint: What promise did onSaveInstanceState make, and what would your late commit do to that promise?

scenarios.title: The recycled-view bug
scenarios.situation: Framework round. A RecyclerView shows the wrong avatar flashing on fast scroll before the right one loads — same symptom family as image lists everywhere.
choices: Bind defensively: in onBindViewHolder set a placeholder/clear the image immediately, tag the load with the item id, and on completion verify the holder still represents that item before setting — with ListAdapter + DiffUtil so updates are minimal and payload-aware.
Disable view recycling with `setIsRecyclable(false)` — correctness first.
Load images synchronously in onBindViewHolder — ordering guaranteed.
Increase the view cache size so rows are never recycled during scroll.
scenarios.why: Recycling means the ViewHolder outlives its data: an async load started for position 5 completes when the holder shows position 42. The fix is identity-checking the completion (or cancelling in onViewRecycled) plus clearing stale state at bind time. DiffUtil/ListAdapter is the modern baseline — mention it unprompted.
scenarios.hint: When the slow image arrives, how does the holder know whether it still represents the same item?

scenarios.title: Surviving rotation
scenarios.situation: Architecture round. A form loses input on rotation; a download restarts too. The interviewer asks for the full strategy.
scenarios.prompt: What survives what, and where does each piece live?
choices: UI state that must survive config changes lives in a ViewModel (scoped to the activity/fragment lifecycle, survives rotation, cleared on real finish); transient view state uses onSaveInstanceState (survives process death too); the download runs in a lifecycle-aware scope (viewModelScope, or WorkManager if it must survive process death).
Everything in onSaveInstanceState — it is the only sanctioned mechanism.
Set `android:configChanges` and handle rotation manually — ViewModels are overkill.
Static fields — they survive everything including process death.
scenarios.why: The three buckets: config change (ViewModel), process death (saved state / persistent store), permanent (database/files). viewModelScope cancels when the VM clears — perfect for UI-bound work. WorkManager is for 'must complete' work. configChanges is a trap: you inherit every config you did not handle.
scenarios.hint: Rotation destroys the activity but not the process. Process death destroys both. Which mechanism covers each?
objectives: Place state in the right survival bucket

scenarios.title: Deep link into checkout
scenarios.situation: Design round. Marketing wants `shop.app/checkout?promo=SUMMER` to land on checkout with the promo applied, even from a cold start.
choices: An intent filter on the checkout activity (or Navigation deep link) matching the URI pattern, parse and validate the promo in one entry point, route through the normal checkout flow state (never a special-case screen), and handle cold start (build the back stack) vs warm start uniformly.
A special DeepLinkActivity per campaign — each link gets its own screen.
Parse the URI in Application.onCreate and store it in a static — available everywhere.
Deep links cannot carry parameters securely; tell marketing it is impossible.
scenarios.why: The senior points: single entry point with validation (never trust URI params — they are user input), back-stack synthesis on cold start (so Back behaves), and reusing the real flow (the promo is just initial state). App Links verification (assetlinks.json) earns a mention for claiming the domain.
scenarios.hint: Cold start vs warm start: what does Back do in each case, and where does the promo get validated?
objectives: Design deep links as validated entry points

scenarios.title: Process Death at 2 AM
scenarios.situation: QA reports: filling a long form, switching to the camera app, returning — the form is empty and the app restarted. Don't keep activities reproduces it instantly.
scenarios.prompt: What is the diagnosis and fix?
choices: Disable the camera app on test devices.

The Activity was destroyed for memory; the form lived only in memory. Fix: persist form state — rememberSaveable for UI state plus DataStore/Room for anything the user must never lose. ViewModel alone is not enough.
Lock the app to portrait so rotation cannot destroy anything.
Increase the heap so the system never kills the process.
scenarios.why: The correct approach names the mechanism: process death, which ViewModels do not survive. rememberSaveable covers UI state across death; durable user input belongs in persistent storage. Orientation locks do not stop process death, heap size does not prevent the low-memory killer, and the camera app is just the trigger.
scenarios.hint: What survives process death — ViewModel, or only what you persist?
objectives: Distinguish config change from process death
evidence: Form empty after returning from camera; logcat shows process recreated (new PID)

domains.name: Coroutines & Concurrency
domains.summary: Suspend functions, dispatchers, structured concurrency, Flows, StateFlow/SharedFlow, and cooperative cancellation.

scenarios.title: What is a suspend function?
scenarios.situation: Coroutines round. 'Explain suspend functions to someone who only knows threads.'
scenarios.prompt: What is the accurate mental model?
choices: A suspend function can pause without blocking its thread: at a suspension point the thread is freed for other work and the coroutine resumes later (possibly on another thread) — sequential-looking code that is non-blocking underneath, unlike Thread.sleep which holds the thread hostage.
A suspend function runs on a dedicated background thread automatically.
It is syntax sugar for callbacks — identical performance and semantics.
Suspend functions cannot call each other; each one needs its own thread.
scenarios.why: The thread analogy: blocking = thread sits idle holding resources; suspending = thread goes back to the pool. Suspension points are only at suspend calls — no preemption mid-computation, which is why shared state reasoning is easier than with threads. Callers must be coroutines (or builders like launch).
scenarios.hint: When your code hits a suspend call, what happens to the thread — and what happens to your local variables?

scenarios.title: Pick the dispatcher
scenarios.situation: Coroutines round. Three jobs: parse a 5MB JSON, write to Room, update a TextView.
choices: JSON parsing -> Dispatchers.Default (CPU-bound work), Room write -> Dispatchers.IO (blocking I/O; Room's suspend DAOs handle this themselves), TextView -> Dispatchers.Main — and never hardcode: inject dispatchers so tests can swap in a TestDispatcher.
Everything on Dispatchers.IO — IO handles all background work.
Everything on Dispatchers.Main — coroutines are light, threads do not matter.
Dispatchers.Unconfined for all — it resumes wherever, which is fastest.
scenarios.why: Default = CPU-bound (sized to cores), IO = blocking I/O (large pool), Main = UI. Unconfined is a testing footgun (resumes on whatever thread). The testability point lands: hardcoded Dispatchers.IO in a repository makes tests flaky; inject and use StandardTestDispatcher.
scenarios.hint: What resource is each job actually waiting on — CPU, disk/network, or the UI toolkit?
objectives: Match dispatchers to the waiting resource

scenarios.title: One failure should not kill the screen
scenarios.situation: Coroutines round. A screen launches three child coroutines; one throws and cancels the other two. The interviewer wants the others to survive.
scenarios.prompt: What is the fix, and what principle is at play?
choices: Use `supervisorScope` (or a SupervisorJob in the scope): a child's failure does not propagate to siblings — versus regular structured concurrency where one failure cancels the whole scope; still handle each child's exception explicitly.
Wrap each child in try/catch — structured concurrency respects caught exceptions.
Launch each child in GlobalScope — independent scopes never cancel each other.
Set `CoroutineExceptionHandler` on the parent — handlers convert failures to successes.
scenarios.why: Structured concurrency's default (fail-fast, cancel siblings) is right for 'all or nothing' work; supervisorScope is for independent work items. GlobalScope is the banned answer (no lifecycle, leaks). The handler note: CoroutineExceptionHandler only works on root coroutines — a favorite follow-up trap.
scenarios.hint: Are these three jobs one unit of work, or three independent ones — and which scope construct matches that?
objectives: Choose supervisor vs structured failure semantics

scenarios.title: StateFlow vs SharedFlow
scenarios.situation: Flow round. The interviewer asks when you would use each for UI events vs UI state.
choices: StateFlow for state (always has a value, conflates to latest, new collectors get current state immediately — perfect for UiState); SharedFlow for events (no initial value, configurable replay/buffer, one-shot navigation/toast events) — with the caveat that events-via-SharedFlow can be lost on rotation, which is why many teams model events as state.
They are interchangeable — pick whichever name you like.
SharedFlow for state (it replays everything) and StateFlow for events (it conflates duplicates).
LiveData for both — Flows are experimental.
scenarios.why: StateFlow = state holder (value semantics, conflation); SharedFlow = event bus (hot, multicast, replay cache configurable). The rotation-loss caveat on one-shot events is senior-level: a SharedFlow event emitted while no collector is active is gone unless replay > 0 — hence the 'events as state' pattern or Channel-based alternatives.
scenarios.hint: A screen rotates mid-navigation-event. Which flow type still has something to deliver to the new collector, and why might that be a problem?
objectives: Separate state holders from event buses

scenarios.title: The leak that survives the screen
scenarios.situation: Debugging round. A repository launches a coroutine in GlobalScope to poll the server; users report battery drain after leaving the screen.
scenarios.prompt: What is wrong and what is the structured fix?
choices: GlobalScope lives for the app's lifetime — the polling coroutine is never cancelled when the screen dies. Fix: launch in a structured scope tied to the UI lifecycle (viewModelScope, lifecycleScope), make the loop cooperative (check isActive / use cancellable suspend calls), and cancel on clear.
Polling is inherently leaky; replace it with a foreground service that never stops.
The drain is from the network, not the coroutine — batching fixes it without touching scopes.
GlobalScope is fine; the bug must be a missing `delay()` making it a busy loop.
scenarios.why: Cancellation in coroutines is cooperative: cancel() only takes effect at suspension points or explicit checks — a `while(true)` with no suspend call ignores cancellation forever. Structured scopes (viewModelScope auto-cancels onCleared) turn 'remember to cancel' into a lifecycle guarantee. This mirrors the iOS Task-cancellation lesson.
scenarios.hint: What owns the coroutine's lifetime right now — and what should?
objectives: Scope coroutines to lifecycles; cancel cooperatively

scenarios.title: Search as you type
scenarios.situation: Architecture round. Design search-as-you-type over a Flow of query strings hitting a repository.
scenarios.prompt: What is the idiomatic Flow design?
choices: `queryFlow.debounce(300).distinctUntilChanged().flatMapLatest { repo.search(it) }.catch { emit(emptyList()) }.flowOn(Dispatchers.IO).stateIn(viewModelScope, ...)` — debounce input, drop repeats, cancel stale searches on new input (flatMapLatest), contain errors without killing the flow, and expose as StateFlow for the UI.
`queryFlow.collect { repo.search(it) }` launching a new coroutine per keystroke — simple and correct.
Throttle the EditText with a Timer and call the API on the main thread — fewer moving parts.
Cache every keystroke's results in a map — memory is cheap, recomputation is not.
scenarios.why: Each operator earns its place: debounce (wait for pause), distinctUntilChanged (skip repeats), flatMapLatest (cancel stale — the same cancellation theme as the iOS list), catch (flows die on uncaught exceptions), flowOn (context for upstream). stateIn with SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed is the standard ViewModel exposure.
scenarios.hint: When the user types 'a', 'ab', 'abc' quickly, how many network calls fire — and what happens to the first two?
objectives: Compose Flow operators into a search pipeline

scenarios.title: The Cancelled Upload
scenarios.situation: An upload runs in viewModelScope.launch. The user navigates away mid-upload; the upload continues, then crashes trying to update the destroyed screen's state.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct structured-concurrency fix?
choices: Use GlobalScope so the upload is independent of the screen.
Keep the upload in viewModelScope but make the state update null-safe.

Scope the upload to the work's lifetime: if it must survive the screen, move it to a WorkManager worker or an application-scoped repository; screen-scoped state updates flow through StateFlow that the current screen collects.
Disable navigation during uploads.
scenarios.why: The correct approach matches scope to lifetime: viewModelScope cancelling on navigate-away is correct behavior, not a bug — the bug is screen-lifetime work that should outlive the screen. WorkManager (guaranteed) or an application-scoped operation owns the upload; UI updates flow through state the current screen collects. GlobalScope abandons cancellation; null-safety hides the lifecycle violation; locking navigation punishes users.
scenarios.hint: Whose lifetime should the upload have — the screen's, or the work's?
objectives: Scope work to its true lifetime
evidence: Upload callback touches destroyed Fragment's binding after navigate-away

domains.name: Persistence on Android
domains.summary: DataStore, Room, migrations, and scoped storage — matching each data kind to its store.

scenarios.title: Goodbye SharedPreferences
scenarios.situation: Persistence round. The app stores settings and a session token in SharedPreferences. The interviewer asks what you would change.
choices: Migrate to DataStore (Preferences DataStore for settings — async, transactional, no blocking reads); move the token out of prefs entirely into EncryptedSharedPreferences or the Keystore-backed store — plain prefs are unencrypted XML.
Keep SharedPreferences — it is stable and DataStore is beta.
Store everything in a SQLite table with one row — unified and queryable.
Use static fields — fastest access, no disk I/O.
scenarios.why: SharedPreferences' sins: synchronous disk I/O on the UI thread (ANRs), no error signaling, no transactions, unencrypted XML. DataStore fixes the mechanics (protobuf or preferences, Flow-based, transactional); EncryptedSharedPreferences/Keystore fixes the secrecy. The token-in-plaintext-prefs is the security finding to name first.
scenarios.hint: What does a SharedPreferences read do to the calling thread — and what does the file look like to anyone with a backup?

scenarios.title: Room basics
scenarios.situation: Persistence round. 'Design the local cache for a product catalog with categories.'
scenarios.prompt: What are the Room building blocks?
choices: `@Entity` data classes (tables), `@Dao` interfaces (queries as functions, suspend or Flow-returning), `@Database` abstract class tying them together — with `@Relation`/embedded for category joins, and the DAO as the single access point the repository talks to.
One `@Entity` per screen — tables should mirror UI.
Raw SQLiteOpenHelper — Room is abstraction overhead.
Store the catalog as JSON in DataStore — Room is only for huge datasets.
scenarios.why: Room is SQLite with compile-time query verification — bad SQL fails the build, not the user. DAOs returning Flow give reactive queries for free; @Transaction guards multi-statement consistency; TypeConverters handle non-primitive columns. The interview check: entities model data, not screens.
scenarios.hint: Where does a SQL typo surface — at compile time or on a user's device?

scenarios.title: Room migration
scenarios.situation: Persistence round. V2 adds a non-null column to the products table. Users have V1 databases.
choices: Write an explicit `Migration(1, 2)` with `ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN ... NOT NULL DEFAULT ...` (SQLite requires a default for non-null adds on existing rows), bump the version, and test with a real V1 database — destructive fallback only as a last resort, never silent data loss.
Bump the version and let Room infer it — migrations are automatic.
Use `fallbackToDestructiveMigration()` — users can re-download.
Delete the database file on upgrade — clean slate, no migration code.
scenarios.why: Room validates migrations: a missing or wrong Migration crashes at runtime, and auto-migration covers only simple cases. Test migrations with the room-testing artifact against exported schemas. The product question to raise: is wiping user data acceptable? Usually no — hence explicit migrations.
scenarios.hint: Existing rows need a value for the new non-null column. Where does it come from?

scenarios.title: Saving a photo on Android 14
scenarios.situation: Framework round. The app saves edited photos. The interviewer asks how, given scoped storage.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct modern approach?
choices: Write via MediaStore into the shared collection (no storage permission needed for your own files on 10+; request READ_MEDIA_IMAGES only to read others'), or keep app-private files in app-specific storage — never request broad storage permissions or use legacy external paths.
Request WRITE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE and write to /sdcard/Photos — it has always worked.
Ask for MANAGE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE — simplest, covers everything.
Save to the app's private dir and tell users to find it with a file manager.
scenarios.why: Scoped storage (10+) ended shared-filesystem free-for-all: MediaStore for media collections, Storage Access Framework for user-picked documents, app-specific dirs for private files. Permission minimalism is graded — requesting broad access you do not need is a review and interview red flag.
scenarios.hint: Whose files are you writing — yours alone, or the user's shared collection? The answer picks the API.

scenarios.title: Offline-first sync conflicts
scenarios.situation: System design. Two devices edit the same product offline; both sync later.
scenarios.prompt: What conflict strategy do you present?
choices: State the options with tradeoffs: last-write-wins (simple, loses data), field-level merge (better UX, more code), tombstones for deletes (so a delete syncs instead of resurrecting), version vectors/CRDTs (correct, heavy) — recommend one for the product's data (e.g. LWW for catalog, merge for user content) and show the sync protocol (delta sync with server timestamps, idempotent upserts).
Server always wins — clients are untrusted anyway.
Whichever syncs last wins — conflicts are rare, do not over-engineer.
Lock the record server-side during offline edits — prevents conflicts entirely.
scenarios.why: The graded move is refusing a single global answer: different data wants different strategies. Tombstones deserve emphasis — without them, deletes vanish on sync and rows resurrect. Idempotency (retry-safe upserts) and delta sync (not full re-download) round out the senior answer.
scenarios.hint: Device A deletes a product while device B edits it offline. What does each device's sync payload need to contain for this to resolve sanely?
objectives: Present conflict strategies per data type

scenarios.title: Choosing the store
scenarios.situation: Design round. The app needs: user settings, an auth token, a 20k-row offline catalog, and cached images.
scenarios.prompt: Assign each to its store and defend it.
choices: Settings -> DataStore Preferences (typed, async, transactional); token -> EncryptedSharedPreferences/Keystore (encrypted, access-controlled); catalog -> Room (queryable, indexed, migrations); images -> disk cache via Coil's disk cache or app storage with an LRU policy (never the database).
Room for everything — one store, one API.
DataStore for everything — modern and simple.
Files for everything — databases are overkill on mobile.
scenarios.why: The ladder again, Android edition: each store's superpower (DataStore: async prefs; Keystore: secrecy; Room: queries; disk: blobs) matched to the data's need. The classic trap is BLOBs in SQLite — it bloats the DB, slows queries, and complicates migrations; images belong on disk with paths in the DB.
scenarios.hint: Which of these four needs to answer 'give me all X where Y' — and which just needs 'give me the value for this key'?
objectives: Match each data kind to its store

scenarios.title: The Sync Conflict
scenarios.situation: A field technician edits a work order offline. Meanwhile, dispatch edits the same order on the web. Both sync. Your current code: last-write-wins silently.
scenarios.prompt: What is the right conflict handling?
choices: Define a per-entity conflict policy: surface the conflict to the user with both versions for the work-order notes (merge UI), use server-wins for dispatch-assigned fields, and log every conflict for audit. Never silently discard a technician's field data.
Reject the second write with an error.
Lock the record on the server whenever anyone opens it.
Keep last-write-wins — it is simple and usually fine.
scenarios.why: The correct approach treats conflicts as domain decisions, not technical defaults: field data entered offline is the technician's work product — silently discarding it destroys trust and data. Per-entity policies (merge UI for notes, server-wins for assignments) plus audit logging handle the real cases. Blind rejection and locking do not work offline.
scenarios.hint: Whose data gets silently thrown away under last-write-wins?
evidence: Technician's 2-hour offline notes overwritten by dispatch's status change; no audit trail

domains.name: App Architecture & Testing
domains.summary: MVVM, repository, Hilt, offline-first, UDF, and testing ViewModels with virtual time.

scenarios.title: Why MVVM on Android?
scenarios.situation: Architecture round. 'Why does the Android community default to MVVM?'
scenarios.prompt: What is the real reason, not the slogan?
choices: The ViewModel survives configuration changes while activities/fragments do not — so UI state and in-flight work live somewhere rotation-safe; the View exposes state (UiState) and events flow up, which also makes the logic unit-testable without Robolectric or devices.
Google mandates it — Play Store rejects MVC apps.
MVVM is faster at runtime than MVC — data binding skips the main thread.
It is just naming: MVVM, MVC, and MVP are identical on Android.
scenarios.why: The lifecycle argument is the honest one: activities die on rotation, ViewModels do not — that single fact drives the whole pattern. UDF (unidirectional data flow: events up, state down) is the discipline that keeps it sane. Testability without Android framework classes is the second pillar.
scenarios.hint: What dies on rotation, what survives — and where would you rather your loaded data live?

scenarios.title: The repository pattern
scenarios.situation: Architecture round. Screens currently call the API and the database directly.
scenarios.prompt: What does introducing a repository buy you?
choices: A single source-of-truth boundary: the UI asks the repository for data and the repository decides (cache-first, network-first, refresh policies) — screens stop knowing where data lives, offline behavior becomes one policy instead of N ad-hoc ones, and tests fake one interface.
It is a required Room annotation — databases need repositories to compile.
It makes network calls faster by pooling connections.
Nothing measurable; it is ceremony for large teams.
scenarios.why: Repository = 'the app's data API'. The decision logic inside (when to hit network, when to serve cache, how to merge) is the product's offline policy in one place. Expose Flows so the UI reacts to cache updates that arrive after a network refresh — the reactive single-source-of-truth payoff.
scenarios.hint: When product says 'show cached data instantly, refresh in background,' how many screens implement that logic today — and after a repository?
objectives: Centralize data decisions in a repository

scenarios.title: Unidirectional data flow
scenarios.situation: Architecture round. A screen has state scattered across five mutable fields updated from callbacks.
scenarios.prompt: How does UDF fix it, and what is the event/state split?
choices: Single `UiState` data class held in a StateFlow; UI renders it; user actions arrive as events (sealed interface) to one `onEvent` entry point that reduces to a new state — one render function of one state object, no partial updates, state changes replayable and testable.
Make all five fields `var` in the fragment — fewer abstractions, direct updates.
Two-way data binding on every field — the framework syncs everything.
Store state in the Application object — globally visible, always consistent.
scenarios.why: UDF's power is the single reduction point: every state change flows through one function you can log, test, and time-travel. Events (one-shot: navigation, toasts) stay separate from state (persistent: list contents) — conflating them is the classic bug (toast re-firing on rotation).
scenarios.hint: If you logged every state transition for a bug report, how many places would you instrument — before and after UDF?

scenarios.title: Hilt scoping
scenarios.situation: DI round. Two ViewModels need the same repository instance; a per-screen analytics tracker must not leak across screens.
scenarios.prompt: How do you scope these with Hilt?
choices: Repository: `@Singleton` (or an activity-retained scope if it holds UI-bound caches) so both ViewModels share one instance and one cache; tracker: unscoped or `@ActivityScoped`/`@ViewModelScoped` so it dies with the screen — and you can articulate why singletons of stateful things are a testability and memory smell.
Everything `@Singleton` — one instance is always simplest.
New instance per injection — sharing state is a bug source.
Static fields instead of Hilt — DI frameworks are overhead.
scenarios.why: Scoping = lifetime control. The interview check: does the candidate connect scope to lifecycle (who creates, who destroys) and to testability (singletons make tests order-dependent)? Constructor injection as the default, Hilt modules for interfaces/third-party types.
scenarios.hint: Who should destroy the analytics tracker, and when — and what breaks if the repository is recreated per ViewModel?

scenarios.title: Test the ViewModel
scenarios.situation: Testing round. `SearchViewModel` debounces queries and calls a repository. 'Make it unit-testable.'
choices: Inject the repository (interface) and a CoroutineDispatcher; in tests use a fake repository plus `StandardTestDispatcher` with `runTest` — advance virtual time past the debounce (`advanceTimeBy(300)`), assert the emitted UiState sequence with Turbine; no real delays, no network, deterministic.
Test against the real repository and staging API — fakes lie.
Use `Thread.sleep(500)` in tests to wait out the debounce — simple and honest.
ViewModels cannot be unit tested; use Espresso for everything.
scenarios.why: The trio: inject dispatchers (virtual time), fake the repository (deterministic data), Turbine (assert flow emissions in order). runTest skips delays automatically — tests run in milliseconds. Also test the sad paths: repository throws -> Error state; rapid queries -> only latest searched.
scenarios.hint: How do you test a 300ms debounce without waiting 300ms — and what breaks if the dispatcher is hardcoded?
objectives: Test ViewModels with virtual time + Turbine

scenarios.title: Offline-first messaging app
scenarios.situation: System design. 'Design the Android client for an offline-first messaging app.' 20 minutes.
choices: Room as source of truth; repository merging local + network; WorkManager outbox for sends (survives process death, retries with backoff); socket/FCM for inbound with delta sync on reconnect; UI as StateFlow of UiState with optimistic message states (sending/sent/failed); conflict story for edits/deletes.
Poll the server every 5 seconds and render responses — simple and robust.
Keep messages in memory and refetch on launch — offline is an edge case.
One giant activity holding a socket — fewer layers, fewer bugs.
scenarios.why: Same graded pieces as any offline-first design: source of truth, outbox pattern, sync semantics, optimistic UI. Android-specific: WorkManager for guaranteed sends, FCM for wakeup, Doze mode implications for sockets (hence FCM + delta sync, not a persistent socket). Draw the layers and trace one send.
scenarios.hint: The user hits send in a tunnel. Walk me through every component that touches that message before it shows 'sent'.

scenarios.title: The God ViewModel
scenarios.situation: CheckoutViewModel is 900 lines: it calls Retrofit directly, formats currency, manages a 12-field form state, and handles navigation. Tests are impossible and every change breaks something.
choices: Split it into two ViewModels: CheckoutViewModel and CheckoutViewModel2.

Extract layers: a repository behind an interface for data, use cases for business rules (pricing, validation), keep the ViewModel as a thin state holder exposing one UI state; move navigation to one-shot events. Then unit-test each layer.
Rewrite the screen in a different architecture library.
Add comments explaining each section.
scenarios.why: The correct approach restores the layering: the ViewModel becomes a thin orchestrator over testable units — repository for data, use cases for rules, single UI state, events for navigation. Splitting into two ViewModels duplicates the problem; a library rewrite keeps the 900 lines; comments document the mess instead of fixing it.
scenarios.hint: What does each line actually do — data, rules, or UI state?
evidence: CheckoutViewModel.kt: 900 lines; imports retrofit2, java.text.NumberFormat, android.content.Intent

domains.name: Guided App Build
domains.summary: Scope a take-home, structure modules, build the networking layer, and self-review like the grader.

scenarios.title: Scoping the take-home
scenarios.situation: Take-home round. 4 hours: 'Build a GitHub repo browser for Android.'
choices: One polished vertical slice: repo list (paging), detail, search with debounce, full state matrix (loading/empty/error/offline), one architecture (MVVM + repository), ViewModel tests, and a README with decisions and cut scope — depth and judgment over feature count.
Every GitHub feature: repos, gists, notifications, settings — breadth wins.
Pixel-perfect custom animations first — delight is memorable.
Skip tests and README — reviewers only run the APK.
scenarios.why: Same rubric logic as any take-home: reviewers grade decision quality under constraint. Android-specific signals: proper lifecycle handling (rotation keeps state), no leaked coroutines, and Material basics right. Timebox and name what you cut.
scenarios.hint: What does the reviewer learn from your README that the APK cannot show them?
objectives: Scope take-homes to a polished slice

scenarios.title: Module structure
scenarios.situation: Build round. Greenfield app, growing team. How do you structure it?
scenarios.prompt: How do you structure the project?
choices: Feature modules (feature-search, feature-detail) over shared core (core-network, core-data, core-ui), dependencies pointing one way (features -> core), public API surfaces minimal — navigable now, extractable to dynamic features later.
One module, packages by layer — modules are premature optimization.
One package per screen class — maximum locality.
Mirror the navigation graph as modules — navigation is the architecture.
scenarios.why: Feature-first grouping: a new hire opens one module and sees a vertical slice. The one-way dependency rule keeps extraction mechanical. Mention build-time wins (parallel compilation, cacheability) as the scaling argument — interviewers like the engineering-economics angle.
scenarios.hint: A new hire fixes a search bug. How much of the codebase must they understand first?
objectives: Structure by feature, depend one way

scenarios.title: Networking with Retrofit
scenarios.situation: Build round. Design the networking layer.
scenarios.prompt: What does a strong Retrofit setup look like?
choices: Retrofit interface per API area with suspend functions returning typed models (Moshi/kotlinx.serialization converter), OkHttp with auth interceptor + logging interceptor (debug only), a typed error mapping layer, and the repository — not screens — owning call/caching policy; inject for tests with MockWebServer.
HttpURLConnection in each ViewModel — no dependencies, full control.
One giant Retrofit interface with 200 methods — discoverable.
String URLs at call sites — the backend docs are the source of truth.
scenarios.why: Suspend functions make Retrofit calls main-safe and cancellable; interceptors centralize auth/logging; converters centralize parsing. MockWebServer gives true HTTP-level tests. The error-mapping layer (HTTP codes -> domain errors) is the senior detail — screens should never see a 401.
scenarios.hint: When auth headers rotate, how many files change — and what does a screen see when the token expires?

scenarios.title: Compose state hoisting
scenarios.situation: Build round. A search screen's composables each hold their own query state and they disagree.
scenarios.prompt: What is the fix, and the rule behind it?
choices: Hoist state up: state lives in the ViewModel (or the lowest common parent), composables receive state + event lambdas and stay stateless — 'state down, events up'; `remember` only for truly local UI state (scroll position, text field draft).
Give every composable its own `remember` state — locality is clean.
Use a global mutable state object — everything stays in sync trivially.
Pass the ViewModel into every composable — direct access, no plumbing.
scenarios.why: Hoisting makes composables predictable and previewable: same inputs, same UI. rememberSaveable survives rotation for UI state; ViewModel survives for business state. The test: can you @Preview this composable with fake data? If not, it is not hoisted enough.
scenarios.hint: Two composables show different queries. Who owns the truth — and how would you preview the screen?

scenarios.title: Finding jank
scenarios.situation: Build round. The list stutters on low-end devices. One hour.
choices: Profile with the Android Profiler / Perfetto: find the hot frame work (overdraw, heavy composition, image decode on main, allocations in bind), fix the measured cause (remember expensive computations, lazy layouts, Coil image pipeline, baseline profiles), re-measure — numbers before and after.
Rewrite in Views — Compose is the obvious cause.
Reduce image resolution globally — fewer pixels, less work.
Wrap bind code in `withContext(Dispatchers.IO)` — background everything.
scenarios.why: Same measurement discipline: profile, fix the measured bottleneck, re-measure. Compose specifics: unstable parameters causing excess recomposition (Layout Inspector / composition counts), remember for derived state, LazyColumn keys, Baseline Profiles for startup. Quote frame-time numbers.
scenarios.hint: What tells you whether the stutter is CPU, GPU overdraw, or GC churn — before you change code?
objectives: Profile jank; fix the measured cause

scenarios.title: Self code review
scenarios.situation: Build round. 30 minutes before submitting the take-home.
choices: Read the diff: no `!!`, no hardcoded dispatchers, no leaked scopes (GlobalScope), rotation preserves state, airplane mode shows the error state with retry, no API keys committed, README covers setup/decisions/cut scope — then submit.
Add more features — bigger diffs impress.
Reformat everything — fresh style signals care.
Submit now — self-review adds nothing.
scenarios.why: The first-five-minutes rule applies: clean diff, handled edge states, no secrets, README preempting questions. Android-specific checks (rotation, process death via 'Don't keep activities', no committed google-services.json secrets) show platform maturity.
scenarios.hint: Turn on 'Don't keep activities' and rotate with airplane mode on. What breaks?
objectives: Review your diff like the grader

domains.name: Mock Interview Circuit
domains.summary: Full-loop rehearsal: rapid-fire fundamentals, whiteboard coding, ANR triage under time, behavioral STAR.

scenarios.title: Explain coroutines in 60 seconds
scenarios.situation: Phone screen. 'Explain Kotlin coroutines to a backend engineer who knows threads.'
choices: Lightweight concurrency: suspend functions pause without blocking threads, so thousands of coroutines share a small pool; structured scopes tie lifetimes to UI lifecycles (viewModelScope), dispatchers pick the thread pool, and cancellation is cooperative — sequential-looking code, non-blocking underneath.
Coroutines are Kotlin's threads — one coroutine equals one thread.
Coroutines are a UI framework for animations.
They are identical to RxJava, just renamed.
scenarios.why: The backend framing wants the contrast with threads (cheap, non-blocking suspension) plus the Android payoff (lifecycle-bound scopes kill leaks). Land dispatchers and cooperative cancellation in one breath each — that is the whole 60 seconds.
scenarios.hint: What happens to the thread at a suspension point — and who guarantees the coroutine dies with the screen?

scenarios.title: Whiteboard: debounce in Kotlin
scenarios.situation: Coding round. 'Debounce search input: 300ms after the last keystroke.'
choices: `queryFlow.debounce(300).flatMapLatest { repo.search(it) }` collected in viewModelScope — or manually: keep a `Job?`, cancel it per keystroke, launch a new one with `delay(300)`; both cancel stale work, which is the actual requirement.
`Thread.sleep(300)` on the main thread per keystroke — delays accumulate naturally.
Fire on every keystroke; the server deduplicates.
A while loop checking `System.currentTimeMillis()` — precise, no dependencies.
scenarios.why: Debounce = cancel previous, schedule new — same theme as iOS. The Flow one-liner shows fluency; the manual Job version shows understanding. flatMapLatest adds stale-search cancellation for free. Mention distinctUntilChanged unprompted for the extra point.
scenarios.hint: What must happen to the previous pending search when a new keystroke arrives?

scenarios.title: ANR under time pressure
scenarios.situation: Onsite debugging. Users report ANRs on a form screen; you have the Play Console stack traces and 10 minutes.
choices: Read the main-thread stack in the ANR trace: find what blocks it (disk I/O, lock, heavy parse, Binder call) — ANR = main thread unresponsive ~5s on input; form the hypothesis from the trace, reproduce with StrictMode on, move the work off-main (or cache it), verify with a stress repro.
Increase the ANR timeout in the manifest — fewer reports, same app.
Show a loading spinner during the block — users tolerate waits they can see.
The traces are sampled and unreliable; ignore them and rewrite the screen.
scenarios.why: Method over fix, same as any debugging round: the trace names the blocker, StrictMode catches it in dev, and the fix is moving work (or removing it — cache, lazy-load). Narrate hypotheses as you rule them out. Bonus: mention ApplicationExitInfo / vitals for production signal.
scenarios.hint: The trace shows the main thread parked inside a `read()` call. What does that tell you in one sentence?
objectives: Triage ANRs from the main-thread trace

scenarios.title: Your hardest bug
scenarios.situation: Behavioral. 'Tell me about the hardest bug you fixed on Android.'
choices: STAR compressed: the symptom and why it was hard (device-specific, race, production-only), systematic narrowing (what you ruled out), root cause, fix plus guard (test, StrictMode, monitoring) — ending with the process change it caused.
Five minutes of deep technical detail — depth proves skill.
Pick a trivial bug to look fast.
Say you have never had a hard bug — refreshing honesty.
scenarios.why: Same grading as any behavioral: structure and growth, not impressiveness. Quantify: crash rate, devices affected, days to root cause, lines changed. The process-change ending is what interviewers remember.
scenarios.hint: What did this bug change about how you work?

scenarios.title: Design a feed
scenarios.situation: System design onsite. 'Design the Android client for a social feed.' 30 minutes.
choices: Data flow: Room as source of truth, repository with paging (Paging 3) over network+db, ViewModel exposing UiState via StateFlow, RecyclerView/Compose lazy list with DiffUtil, image pipeline (Coil) with cancellation on recycle, pull-to-refresh and retry states — then deep-dives (offline, prefetch, memory).
Start with the visual design — feeds are UI problems.
Draw the server architecture — backend matters more.
List every feature first — completeness over depth.
scenarios.why: Paging 3 is the expected answer for infinite lists (it handles the DB+network boundary); the rest mirrors the iOS feed: source of truth, cancellation, state matrix. Timebox: clarify, core flow, deep-dives. Name what you defer.
scenarios.hint: Trace one page of data from network to pixel — where is it cached, and what happens on rotation mid-load?
objectives: Lead client system design from data flow

scenarios.title: The full loop simulation
scenarios.situation: Final prep. Onsite in 3 days: coding, architecture, debugging, behavioral.
choices: Day 1: timed Kotlin reps (debounce, LRU, Flow pipelines) out loud; Day 2: architecture narrations (your app's architecture, offline-first) recorded and critiqued; Day 3: light review + STAR stories + sleep — no new topics the night before; one peer mock beats ten solo hours.
200 LeetCode hards — volume separates candidates.
Memorize API signatures — recall speed is the bottleneck.
Rest entirely — cramming hurts.
scenarios.why: Same principle: train the test format. Android loops add system-design and 'explain the framework' rounds — rehearse those narrations specifically, not just algorithms.
scenarios.hint: Which loop section is your weakest — does the plan spend the most time there?
objectives: Train the test format, not just the material

domains.name: Systems Anatomy: Seeing Systems as Living Flows
domains.description: Learn to see Android Interview as living systems — not static diagrams, but moving sequences where every part connects. Master systems thinking for exams and interviews.

scenarios.title: The Kotlin Core Mystery
scenarios.situation: Users report that Kotlin Core is not working correctly. The obvious checks pass — the components are online, basic connectivity works. You need to think in systems, not symptoms.
scenarios.prompt: Using the systems anatomy method (whole → cut open → step through → pull apart), how would you systematically trace a failure in Kotlin Core?
choices: Walk the full journey: start from the trigger, verify each handoff in sequence, check dependencies at every step, and isolate where the flow breaks — then examine that specific layer
Restart all components — Kotlin Core issues are always fixed by restarting
Check the most common cause from memory and apply that fix immediately
Escalate to senior support — Kotlin Core is too complex to troubleshoot systematically
scenarios.why: Systems thinking means tracing the living flow: (1) Whole: what is Kotlin Core supposed to do end-to-end? (2) Cut open: what are the layers/stages? (3) Step through: verify each handoff — where does the expected output diverge from actual? (4) Pull apart: isolate the broken layer and examine it in detail. This method works for any Kotlin Core failure in Android Interview.
scenarios.hint: Don't jump to the fix. First map the journey, then find where it breaks.
objectives: Apply systems anatomy to Kotlin Core
evidence: All Kotlin Core components report 'online'. Basic health checks pass.
Functionality is broken despite green status indicators. The failure is in the flow, not the components.

scenarios.prompt: Using the systems anatomy method (whole → cut open → step through → pull apart), how would you systematically trace a failure in Android Framework?
choices: Walk the full journey: start from the trigger, verify each handoff in sequence, check dependencies at every step, and isolate where the flow breaks — then examine that specific layer
Restart all components — Android Framework issues are always fixed by restarting
Check the most common cause from memory and apply that fix immediately
Escalate to senior support — Android Framework is too complex to troubleshoot systematically
scenarios.why: Systems thinking means tracing the living flow: (1) Whole: what is Android Framework supposed to do end-to-end? (2) Cut open: what are the layers/stages? (3) Step through: verify each handoff — where does the expected output diverge from actual? (4) Pull apart: isolate the broken layer and examine it in detail. This method works for any Android Framework failure in Android Interview.

domains.name: Start Here: Ground Floor

scenarios.title: Navigate the Bootcamp
scenarios.situation: You have 30 days before your assessment. You open the bootcamp and see 15 domains, a terminal, drills, and a mock. You feel overwhelmed.
scenarios.prompt: What is the highest-leverage first week plan?
choices: Complete Start Here, then work the first three core domains in order — lessons with knowledge checks, then their scenarios, then one lab. Establish the daily loop before widening.
Take the full mock on day one to 'see where you stand,' then study randomly.
Read every lesson in all 15 domains first, then attempt scenarios in week three.
Skip lessons entirely and grind drills — speed matters more than understanding.
scenarios.why: The correct approach is the structured loop: Start Here orients you, then sequential domains build the foundation scenarios assume. The mock on day one wastes your only baseline and demoralizes; random study leaves gaps the assessment will find. Drills without understanding produce fast wrong answers.
scenarios.hint: Think about what the scenarios assume you already know.
evidence: 30 days available, ~2 hours per day on weekdays

scenarios.title: When You Get Stuck
scenarios.situation: You have failed the same scenario three times. The explanation makes sense when you read it, but you keep choosing wrong under time pressure.
choices: Drop back to the lesson: re-read the concepts, write out the decision process in your own words, then re-attempt the scenario untimed before going timed again.
Keep re-attempting the scenario until you memorize the right answer.
Skip it and move on — one scenario will not decide the assessment.
Look up the answer online and move faster through the rest.
scenarios.why: The correct approach treats repeated failure as a signal: the mental model is broken, not the memory. Rebuilding from the lesson concepts — in your own words — repairs the model. Memorizing the answer passes one scenario and fails the next variation. The assessment tests patterns, not instances.
scenarios.hint: Is the problem memory or the underlying mental model?
objectives: Repair mental models from lesson concepts
evidence: Scenario failed 3x: same wrong choice twice, different wrong choice once

domains.name: Android Testing

scenarios.title: The Flaky Suite
scenarios.situation: Your Espresso suite passes locally but fails randomly on CI — different tests each run. The team wants to add retry logic.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct first move?
choices: Audit background work Espresso cannot track: custom executors, raw threads, and unregistered IdlingResources. Make async work visible to the framework instead of masking timing with retries.
Run the suite only on faster emulators to reduce timing variance.
Mark the flaky tests @Ignore and file tickets to fix them later.
Add retry-on-failure to CI — flakes are environmental, retries keep the build green.
scenarios.why: The correct approach fixes the synchronization root cause: Espresso is deterministic when it can see all async work. Retries and faster emulators mask the timing; @Ignore surrenders coverage. Find the untracked executor or missing IdlingResource and the flakes disappear.
scenarios.hint: What does Espresso synchronize with automatically — and what escapes it?
evidence: 12 failures in 50 runs, no single test fails twice

scenarios.title: Where Does This Test Go?
scenarios.situation: You need to test a pure function that calculates cart totals with tax and discount rules. A teammate suggests an Espresso test so it covers the real UI.
choices: Espresso — end-to-end coverage of the real screen is the safest.
A JVM unit test in the test/ source set — pure logic, no framework needed, runs in milliseconds.
An on-device instrumentation test — it uses Android APIs indirectly.
Manual QA — business logic this important deserves human eyes.
scenarios.why: The correct approach puts pure logic at the base of the pyramid: a JVM unit test is fast, deterministic, and precise. Espresso for a tax calculation is slow, indirect, and tests the UI instead of the math. Save instrumentation for what genuinely needs the framework.
scenarios.hint: What does this function actually depend on?
evidence: fun cartTotal(items: List<Item>, taxRate: Double): Money — no Android imports

scenarios.title: Testing the ViewModel
scenarios.situation: Interview question: walk me through how you unit test a ViewModel that exposes a StateFlow of UI state and loads data from a repository.
choices: Test it only through Espresso — ViewModels are UI-adjacent.
Launch the activity with ActivityScenario and assert on the visible text.
Inject a fake repository and a TestDispatcher, collect the StateFlow with Turbine inside runTest, trigger the load, advanceUntilIdle, and assert each emitted state in order.
Mock the ViewModel itself and verify its methods were called.
scenarios.why: The correct approach is the standard pattern: fake repo plus TestDispatcher for determinism, Turbine to assert the emission sequence (Loading then Success/Error), all inside runTest. The other options either test the wrong layer or make the test slow and indirect.
scenarios.hint: What are the two things that make ViewModel tests flaky, and what replaces them?
evidence: class FeedViewModel(repo, dispatcher) — val uiState: StateFlow<FeedUiState>

scenarios.title: The Brittle Suite
scenarios.situation: Refactoring a repository implementation — same public API — breaks 40 unit tests. Every test verifies exact mock interactions.
scenarios.prompt: What went wrong and what is the fix?
choices: The refactor was wrong — revert it to match the tests.
Mock less: use real repositories with a test database everywhere.
The tests are too thorough — delete the redundant ones.

Over-verification: the tests assert implementation details instead of behavior. Rewrite them to assert outcomes (returned values, emitted states) and reserve verify() for cases where the interaction itself is the requirement.
scenarios.why: The correct approach diagnoses the coupling: tests that verify every mock call encode the implementation, so any refactor breaks them. Behavior-focused tests survive implementation changes. Real repositories everywhere would make the suite slow — fakes and outcome assertions are the middle path.
scenarios.hint: What should survive a refactor with an unchanged public API?
evidence: 40 tests fail; production code behavior unchanged per QA

scenarios.title: Testing the DAO
scenarios.situation: You need to verify a Room DAO query with a JOIN and a complex WHERE clause. The query is easy to get subtly wrong.
choices: An instrumentation test using an in-memory Room database: insert known rows, run the DAO query, assert the exact result set.
An Espresso test that navigates to the screen showing the data.
Skip it — Room generates the implementation, so it is already correct.
A JVM unit test with a mocked DAO — fast and simple.
scenarios.why: The correct approach tests the actual SQL: an in-memory Room database on-device runs your real query against known data. A mocked DAO tests nothing about the query. Espresso is too indirect, and Room generates code from your SQL — if your SQL is wrong, the generated code is faithfully wrong.
scenarios.hint: What is the actual risk here — the framework or your SQL?
objectives: Test Room DAOs with in-memory DB
Distinguish framework code from your SQL
evidence: @Query(SELECT ... JOIN ... WHERE ...) — 3-table join with date filters

scenarios.title: CI Test Strategy
scenarios.situation: Your CI pipeline runs the full suite — unit plus 200 Espresso tests — on every pull request. PRs now wait 45 minutes for a green build.
choices: Run everything on every PR — correctness first, developers can wait.
Split the pipeline: fast JVM unit tests plus lint on every PR as the merge gate; the full Espresso suite runs nightly and on release branches. Flaky-prone UI tests never block merging.
Delete the Espresso tests — they are too slow for CI.
Run the suite on fewer API levels to save time.
scenarios.why: The correct approach matches test speed to pipeline stage: unit tests gate PRs in minutes, the slow UI suite runs on a schedule where its signal still matters. Deleting UI tests surrenders critical-journey coverage; fewer API levels is a minor saving that misses the structural problem.
scenarios.hint: Which tests give fast signal, and which give slow-but-valuable signal?
evidence: Unit tests: 3 min. Espresso: 42 min. PRs per day: 15

scenarios.title: The Unintended Redesign
scenarios.situation: A PR changes a shared Button component's padding. All unit and UI tests pass, but the design team later reports the checkout screen looks wrong in production.
scenarios.prompt: What testing layer would have caught this before merge?
choices: Manual QA on every PR touching shared components.
Stricter code review requiring designer approval on all PRs.
A screenshot test on the Button component and key screens — pixel diffs against goldens would have flagged the visual change at PR time.
More Espresso assertions on button text.
scenarios.why: The correct approach adds the visual layer other tests miss: unit and Espresso tests assert behavior and semantics, not pixels. Screenshot tests diff rendered output against goldens, catching unintended visual changes mechanically at PR time. Manual QA and designer review do not scale to every PR; text assertions cannot see padding.
scenarios.hint: Which tests can actually see pixels?
objectives: Place screenshot tests in the pyramid
Catch visual regressions at PR time
evidence: Button padding 16dp -> 12dp; 0 test failures; design reports broken checkout spacing
