domains.name: Android Performance

scenarios.title: The ANR Report
scenarios.situation: Play Console shows ANR rate climbing to 1.8% after your last release — mostly Input dispatching timed out in the feed screen.
scenarios.prompt: What is the most likely cause and the fix?
choices: Increase the ANR timeout in the manifest.
The devices are too slow — raise minSdk to exclude them.
Add more RAM to the test devices.
The feed screen does heavy work on the main thread — image decoding or JSON parsing during scroll/bind. Move it off the main thread, precompute bind values, and re-measure with GPU rendering bars.
scenarios.why: The correct approach reads the ANR literally: input dispatch timed out means the main thread was blocked for 5+ seconds. The feed screen is the suspect — bind-path work is the usual culprit. Timeouts cannot be configured, slow devices are your users, and test-device RAM changes nothing in production.
scenarios.hint: What does Input dispatching timed out actually mean about the main thread?
evidence: ANR rate 0.4% -> 1.8%; 80% in FeedActivity; traces show main thread in BitmapFactory.decodeStream

scenarios.title: The Janky List
scenarios.situation: Users report the product list stutters while scrolling. GPU rendering bars show many frames crossing the 16ms line.
choices: Whether onBindViewHolder does decoding, formatting, or allocation — move that work out of the bind path, enable setHasFixedSize, and flatten the item layout.
Rewrite the list in OpenGL for maximum performance.
Increase the RecyclerView pool size to 500.
Disable animations globally.
scenarios.why: The correct approach starts with the bind path — the overwhelmingly common cause — and the cheap structural fixes. A rewrite is disproportionate before diagnosis, a 500-view pool wastes memory, and disabling animations hides the symptom while degrading UX.
scenarios.hint: What runs once per item per frame during a scroll?
evidence: Jank worsens with images; text-only lists scroll smoothly

scenarios.title: The Growing Memory Graph
scenarios.situation: The memory profiler shows a staircase: memory climbs on every screen rotation and never returns. LeakCanary flags the detail Activity.
choices: Increase the heap with largeHeap=true.
A long-lived reference holds the Activity — likely a static field, an unregistered listener, or a non-static inner class. Read LeakCanary's reference chain to find the holder and break it.
Android is caching the activities for faster relaunch — this is normal.
The garbage collector is lazy — call System.gc() after rotation.
scenarios.why: The correct approach trusts the evidence: retained instances after rotation plus LeakCanary's reference chain is a leak, not caching. System.gc() does not fix reachability, and largeHeap postpones the OOM while the leak continues. Find the holder in the chain and release it.
scenarios.hint: If the GC could reach it, would LeakCanary flag it as retained?
objectives: Fix the holder not the symptom

scenarios.title: The Slow Cold Start
scenarios.situation: Cold start takes 2.8 seconds. Application.onCreate initializes analytics, crash reporting, DI, and prefetches user data — all before the first frame.
choices: Buy faster phones for the QA team.
Move the init into the first Activity's onCreate instead.

Defer everything not needed for the first frame: init critical path synchronously, post the rest to a Choreographer frame callback or background thread, and add a Baseline Profile for the startup journey.
Show a splash screen so the wait feels intentional.
scenarios.why: The correct approach shrinks the critical path: only first-frame work runs before first frame. A splash screen decorates the wait, faster phones do not change user devices, and moving init to the Activity keeps it on the critical path. Baseline Profiles then compile the hot path ahead of time.
scenarios.hint: What must happen before the first frame, and what merely happens to be there?
evidence: onCreate: analytics 400ms, DI 600ms, prefetch 900ms network on main thread

scenarios.title: The Battery Complaints
scenarios.situation: Reviews complain your app drains battery. Battery Historian shows frequent network wake-ups every 5 minutes around the clock.
choices: Poll more often so each poll transfers less data.
Hold a partial wake lock during polls to finish faster.
Tell users to disable battery optimization for the app.
Replace the polling AlarmManager with WorkManager — batched, constraint-aware (unmetered, charging) — or switch to FCM push so the radio wakes only when there is real data.
scenarios.why: The correct approach stops waking the radio on a fixed timer: WorkManager lets the OS batch your work into maintenance windows, and FCM push eliminates polling entirely. More frequent polls multiply wake-ups; wake locks and exemption requests fight the OS instead of cooperating with Doze.
scenarios.hint: What does each 5-minute wake-up cost, and who pays it?
evidence: Mobile radio active 40x/hour; app uid responsible for 70% of wake-ups

scenarios.title: The OOM Crash
scenarios.situation: Crash reports show OutOfMemoryError in the gallery screen on low-RAM devices. The screen loads full-resolution camera photos into a grid of small thumbnails.
choices: Downsample at decode time: read dimensions with inJustDecodeBounds, compute inSampleSize for the thumbnail size, and decode the smaller bitmap. Cache the thumbnails, not the full images.
Catch OutOfMemoryError and retry the load.
Set largeHeap=true in the manifest.
Load the images on a background thread.
scenarios.why: The correct approach decodes to the view size: a 4000px photo in a 200dp thumbnail wastes roughly 60x the memory, and no threading change fixes that arithmetic. Catching OOM is unreliable, largeHeap just moves the crash, and background threads do not shrink bitmaps.
scenarios.hint: How many pixels does the ImageView actually display?
evidence: OOM allocating 48MB bitmap; device heap 192MB; thumbnail views are 200dp

scenarios.title: The 180MB Download
scenarios.situation: Your app's download size is 180MB. Install conversion in emerging markets is poor and Play warns about large downloads over mobile data.
scenarios.prompt: What is the highest-leverage size reduction plan?
choices: Remove the settings screen to save space.
Switch to AAB if not already, enable resource shrinking, filter to arm64-v8a, convert PNGs to WebP, and move the onboarding video and ML model to on-demand dynamic features.
Ask users to free up storage before installing.
Compress the APK with a stronger zip setting.
scenarios.why: The correct approach attacks the measured top offenders structurally: AAB gives per-device APKs, shrinking strips the unused, ABI filters drop dead architectures, WebP shrinks images, and dynamic features defer the heavy assets. Zip settings barely move already-compressed media; deleting features is not an optimization.
scenarios.hint: What does APK Analyzer say the megabytes actually are?
evidence: native libs 90MB (4 ABIs), PNGs 40MB, onboarding video 25MB, ML model 20MB

domains.description: Profiling, jank-free rendering, memory management, startup time, and battery optimization.

domains.name: Android Security

scenarios.title: The Permission Avalanche
scenarios.situation: Your app requests location, camera, contacts, and microphone at first launch. Denial rates are high and Play reviews complain.
choices: Request each permission in context at the moment of use, explain why with a rationale when previously denied, and degrade gracefully when refused — never demand all permissions up front.
Request them one screen earlier so users are prepared.
Detect denial and exit the app with an explanation.
Move the requests to the onboarding carousel with illustrations.
scenarios.why: The correct approach follows the platform model: in-context requests with rationale convert far better than launch-time avalanches, and graceful degradation keeps users who refuse. Earlier requests, forced exits, and prettier carousels all keep the fundamental mistake — asking before the user understands why.
scenarios.hint: When does the user understand why you need the camera?
evidence: First-launch prompt: 68% deny location; in-context prompt: 22% deny

scenarios.title: The Leaked API Key
scenarios.situation: A backend API key was found hardcoded in your APK on a public forum. Attackers are abusing the endpoint and the key cannot be rotated instantly.
scenarios.prompt: What is the immediate and structural fix?
choices: Embed the key in native code via JNI — much harder to extract.

Immediately: revoke and rotate the key, add rate limiting and anomaly detection server-side. Structurally: move the secret behind your own backend — the app authenticates the user, the server holds the key.
Obfuscate the new key harder with R8 and split it across string resources.
Sue the forum for hosting the key.
scenarios.why: The correct approach accepts the APK is public: any secret shipped in it is compromised by design. Rotation plus server-side controls stop the bleeding; moving secrets behind your backend fixes the architecture. Better hiding (obfuscation, JNI) only delays the next extraction.
scenarios.hint: Is there any place inside the APK an attacker cannot read?
evidence: Key extracted via apktool in under 10 minutes; abuse ongoing

scenarios.title: The Exported Activity
scenarios.situation: A security audit flags your app: an internal debug Activity is exported and accepts extras that trigger test payments in production builds.
choices: Require root to launch it.

Set android:exported=false on every component that does not genuinely serve external callers, strip debug activities from release builds via build variants, and gate test actions behind server-side flags.
Add a password extra to the debug Activity.
Rename the Activity to something obscure.
scenarios.why: The correct approach removes the attack surface: unexported components cannot be invoked externally, and debug code should not ship in release at all. A password extra is security through obscurity on an exported component; renaming and root-gating do not remove the exposure.
scenarios.hint: Who can start an exported Activity?
evidence: 3 exported activities; 2 have intent filters for internal use only

scenarios.title: The Coffee-Shop Attack
scenarios.situation: Your app handles health data. A pentest shows traffic can be intercepted with a proxy CA installed on the device — the app trusts it silently.
choices: Block the app from running on devices with user-installed CAs.
Encrypt the payload with a hardcoded AES key as a second layer.
Show a warning dialog when a proxy is detected.

Add certificate pinning for the API domain via Network Security Config or OkHttp CertificatePinner, with a backup pin and rotation plan — so only your real certificate is trusted even with a rogue CA installed.
scenarios.why: The correct approach is pinning: it binds the connection to your actual certificate, defeating MITM even with a trusted rogue CA. Blocking user CAs breaks enterprise devices, hardcoded AES repeats the leaked-key mistake, and a warning dialog trains users to tap through.
scenarios.hint: What does the app trust today, and what should it trust?
evidence: Charles Proxy with installed CA decrypted all API traffic; no pinning present

scenarios.title: The Backup Surprise
scenarios.situation: Auto Backup restored a user's app data to a new device — including the plain-text auth token from SharedPreferences. The token now lives in their Google Drive backup.
choices: Disable Auto Backup entirely for the app.
Shorten token lifetimes to 5 minutes.
Encrypt the token with a hardcoded key before storing.
Migrate tokens to EncryptedSharedPreferences with a Keystore-backed key and add a fullBackupContent XML that excludes sensitive files — sensitive data should never sit in backups unencrypted.
scenarios.why: The correct approach encrypts at rest and excludes what should not be backed up: EncryptedSharedPreferences protects the token wherever it lands, and backup rules keep key material out of Drive. Disabling backup punishes users, short lifetimes do not fix plaintext storage, and hardcoded keys are extractable.
scenarios.hint: Where else does this token end up besides the device?
evidence: auth_token in default SharedPreferences XML; backup enabled with defaults

scenarios.title: The Repackaged APK
scenarios.situation: A modified version of your app with ads stripped and cheat features circulates on third-party stores. Some users install it and blame you for the bugs.
choices: Detect the repackaged app and brick the user's device.

Layer defenses: Play Integrity attestation gating sensitive actions, runtime signature verification, R8 obfuscation — while enforcing critical rules server-side, since no client check survives a determined reverser.
Sue the third-party stores.
Add a EULA popup forbidding modification.
scenarios.why: The correct approach is defense in depth with honest limits: attestation plus tamper checks raise the cost, but the server is the real boundary — never trust the client for anything valuable. Lawsuits and popups do not stop redistribution; bricking devices is disproportionate and dangerous.
scenarios.hint: What can a repackaged app still not fake?
evidence: Modded APK: package name identical, signature differs, 50k installs

scenarios.title: The Biometric Shortcut
scenarios.situation: A developer implements login with fingerprint as: BiometricPrompt, then on success set a boolean isUnlocked=true and show the vault. A pentest flags it.
scenarios.prompt: What is wrong and what is the correct pattern?
choices: Nothing — the system verified the biometric, so the boolean is fine.
Move the boolean into EncryptedSharedPreferences.

The boolean is bypassable client-side state. Correct pattern: bind approval to a Keystore CryptoObject — the vault decryption key only unlocks inside the authenticated cipher, so there is no boolean to flip.
Require a PIN as well as the biometric.
scenarios.why: The correct approach removes the bypassable decision point: a boolean in memory can be flipped by anyone who controls the process. Crypto-bound auth makes the biometric approval inseparable from the key operation — no approval, no decryption, nothing to bypass. Storing the boolean encrypted does not fix the logic flaw; adding a PIN piles on friction without fixing the architecture.
scenarios.hint: What happens if an attacker flips the boolean?
evidence: Hook flips isUnlocked; vault opens with no biometric

domains.name: Android Publishing

scenarios.title: The Lost Keystore
scenarios.situation: A developer's laptop died with the only copy of the upload keystore. The app uses Play App Signing. The release is due Friday.
choices: Delay the release until the laptop drive is recovered.
Create a new Play listing and ask users to reinstall.
Ship the release unsigned.
Generate a new upload key, register it with Play Console (Play App Signing makes this a supported flow), update CI secrets — the app signing key Google holds is untouched, so users are unaffected.
scenarios.why: The correct approach uses the designed recovery: with Play App Signing, the upload key is replaceable through a Console request — this is exactly why Google holds the app signing key. Drive recovery wastes days, a new listing abandons your users, and unsigned uploads are rejected.
scenarios.hint: Which key do users devices trust — the upload key or the app signing key?
evidence: App Signing enrolled; upload key certificate registered 2024

scenarios.title: The Crash Spike
scenarios.situation: Two hours into a 10% staged rollout, crash-free rate drops from 99.6% to 97.9% with a new crash cluster in the top 5.
choices: Halt the rollout immediately in Play Console, pull the stack traces for the new cluster, fix, and ship a new release — never resume a halted rollout without a fix.
Wait 24 hours — early rollout data is noisy.
Resume to 100% quickly so the fix (when ready) reaches everyone at once.
Roll back to the previous version for the 10% affected.
scenarios.why: The correct approach honors the pre-written halt criteria: a 1.7-point drop plus a new top-5 cluster is unambiguous. Waiting lets the blast radius grow; resuming to 100% maximizes damage; Play staged rollouts halt forward — you fix forward with a new release, not backward.
scenarios.hint: What were your halt criteria, and does this meet them?
evidence: Rollout at 10%; crash-free 99.6% -> 97.9%; new cluster: NullPointerException in CheckoutViewModel

scenarios.title: The versionCode Trap
scenarios.situation: You uploaded versionCode 52 to the internal track, found a bug, and uploaded the fix as versionCode 51 by mistake. Play rejected it.
choices: Upload the fix as a new app listing.
Bump to versionCode 53 and upload the fix — versionCode must always increase; the rejected 51 changes nothing and the numbering continues from the highest uploaded.
Delete versionCode 52 from the track and reuse 51.
Rename versionName to force acceptance.
scenarios.why: The correct approach moves forward: Play orders by versionCode and rejects anything not higher than the max uploaded. Deleting from a track does not always reset the counter, versionName is cosmetic, and a new listing is absurd for a numbering slip.
scenarios.hint: What does Play compare your upload against?
evidence: Error: versionCode 51 < 52 already uploaded to internal track

scenarios.title: The Pre-Launch Warning
scenarios.situation: The pre-launch report flags a crash on a low-RAM device and an accessibility warning about unlabeled buttons — 48 hours before your planned production release.
choices: Ship and fix in the next release.
Exclude low-RAM devices from the release.
Treat the crash as a release blocker: reproduce on a similar device profile, fix, and re-run. Fix the content descriptions too — accessibility warnings are cheap to fix and expensive to ignore.
Ship anyway — pre-launch reports are advisory.
scenarios.why: The correct approach treats automated device testing as the gate it is: a crash on a real device profile is a real crash your users will hit. Advisory-only thinking wastes the testing you already paid for with the upload; excluding devices shrinks your market instead of fixing the bug.
scenarios.hint: Who uses low-RAM devices — edge cases or your market?
evidence: Crash: OOM on 2GB RAM device (8% of install base); 14 buttons missing contentDescription

scenarios.title: The Enterprise Review
scenarios.situation: An enterprise client wants to review your app before it reaches the public Play listing. They need it on 40 devices next week.
choices: Production with a staged rollout at 1%.
Email them the APK directly.
Open testing — they can join like anyone else.
Closed testing track with the client's email list — they install via the Play link, the app never touches production, and you can push review builds fast.
scenarios.why: The correct approach is the closed track: targeted distribution through Play's own install flow, with signing and updates handled. A 1% production rollout exposes the app publicly; emailed APKs bypass Play Protect warnings and update mechanics; open testing invites the whole internet to the review.
scenarios.hint: What does the client actually need — the app, or the app plus Play's install trust?
evidence: 40 devices, mixed personal and corporate, review in 7 days

scenarios.title: The Critical Fix
scenarios.situation: A data-corruption bug is live in production. The fix is uploaded and rolling out, but 60% of users have auto-update off or delayed.
scenarios.prompt: How do you get the fix onto devices fast?
choices: Use the In-App Updates API with IMMEDIATE flow for the affected versions — Play drives a blocking update inside your app — plus a server-side kill switch or minimum-version gate to protect users until they update.
Send a push notification asking users to update.
Wait for the staged rollout to complete.
Publish a blog post explaining the bug.
scenarios.why: The correct approach combines Play's blocking update flow with server-side protection: IMMEDIATE updates prompt inside the app, and a minimum-version gate stops old clients from corrupting more data. A push notification is ignorable, waiting is passive, and a blog post updates nobody's app.
scenarios.hint: What can you control for users who never open the Play Store?
evidence: Corruption bug in v2.3.0 (versionCode 47); 60% of active installs still on 47

scenarios.title: The Rejected Update
scenarios.situation: Your update is rejected: target API level requirement not met, and the Data safety section is flagged as incomplete. The release train is stopped.
choices: Appeal the rejection and explain the timeline pressure.

Bump targetSdkVersion, test the release artifact against behavior changes, complete the Data safety form accurately, and add Play policy checks (target API calendar, data safety, permission declarations) to the release checklist so it never blocks again.
Publish as a new app listing to bypass the requirement.
Remove all permissions to simplify the Data safety form.
scenarios.why: The correct approach fixes both the instance and the system: the target API bump unblocks shipping (with behavior-change testing, since new target levels change runtime behavior), the honest data safety form clears the flag, and the checklist prevents recurrence. Appeals do not waive published requirements; new listings inherit the same rules; stripping permissions breaks features.
scenarios.hint: Is this a one-time fix or a process gap?
evidence: Rejection: targetSdk 33 required (app targets 31); Data safety: 3 undeclared SDK data types

scenarios.prompt: How do you scope the build?
choices: Write the plan first: phases with definitions of done, mapped to bootcamp domains. Start with the smallest working core, then layer on complexity. Document decisions as you go.
Start building immediately — planning wastes lab time.
Attempt the most impressive architecture possible to stand out.
Build whatever is easiest to finish quickly.

lessons.title: Android Engineering Interview Prep — Core concepts
concepts: Android loops test five things: Kotlin precision (null safety, coroutines mental model), framework depth (lifecycles, intents, views), concurrency discipline (dispatchers, Flows, cancellation), architecture judgment (MVVM, repository, offline-first), and visible reasoning under time.
Kotlin's type system is your first line of defense: nullable types, data/sealed classes, and delegation remove whole bug classes — use them, and say why when you do.

The activity/fragment lifecycle is the platform's central fact: things die (rotation, process death) on schedules you do not control. Every state decision is really a survival-bucket decision: ViewModel, saved state, or persistent store.
Coroutines are structured concurrency: scopes own lifetimes, dispatchers match the waiting resource, cancellation is cooperative, and Flows model streams — StateFlow for state, SharedFlow for events.

Architecture is about the arrows: UI renders state, events flow up, the repository owns data decisions, and dependencies point one way. If you can draw the boxes and trace one user action through them, you can answer any architecture question.
The meta-skill is narration: state assumptions, name tradeoffs, timebox whiteboard work, and verify with tests or traces. The thinking is the product; the code is evidence.

example.walkthrough: One ViewModel, five interview themes: injected dispatcher and repository (testability), debounce + distinctUntilChanged + flatMapLatest (stale-search cancellation), catch (flows must not die), and StateFlow exposure for the UI. Narrate each operator's job and you own the coroutines round.

pitfalls: Common trap: `!!` anywhere in written code — interviewers read it as a scheduled NPE.
Common trap: GlobalScope or hardcoded Dispatchers.IO — unstructured lifetimes and untestable code.
Common trap: committing fragment transactions from callbacks without lifecycle awareness — the state-loss crash.
Common trap: answering 'which is better' with a winner instead of tradeoffs, measurement, and a deferral list.
lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Labs tab.

lessons.title: From Static Diagrams to Living Systems
concepts: A textbook diagram shows you one part in isolation — a living systems view shows you how all parts of Android Interview move together in sequence
The four-step systems anatomy method: (1) See the whole in context, (2) Cut it open to reveal layers, (3) Walk through the process step-by-step, (4) Pull apart into labeled pieces
Apply this to any system in this course: start with the trigger action, trace through every component it touches, watch the data flow
Interview/exam power: when asked 'how does X work?', narrate the journey — 'it starts here, then...'. This demonstrates senior-level systems thinking

example.code:
TRIGGER event occurs
  → First system receives it (see the handoff)
  → Processing happens in sequence (watch each step)
  → State changes propagate (follow the ripple)
  → Final outcome delivered

Each arrow is a living handoff, not a static box.
example.walkthrough: This is the 'jet engine cutaway' for your field: instead of memorizing isolated facts, you see the entire flow as a moving sequence. Practice narrating this journey out loud.

pitfalls: Memorizing terms without understanding the processes they participate in
Drawing architecture diagrams as boxes without showing the data flow between them
Answering 'how does X work?' with a definition instead of walking through the sequence
lessons.try_it: Pick any process in this course. Write out the full journey from trigger to outcome, naming every system touched.

lessons.title: Anatomy of Kotlin Core
concepts: Kotlin Core is a multi-step process within Kotlin Core: trace the full sequence from initiation to completion
See it as a journey: identify the trigger, follow each handoff, watch state change at every step
Every step depends on the previous — a failure at any point breaks the chain. Map these dependencies
Connect Kotlin Core to the broader Kotlin Core ecosystem — nothing operates in isolation

example.code:
Step 1: Initiation
  Kotlin Core begins — what triggers it?

Step 2: Processing
  Data flows through — what transforms it?

Step 3: Handoff
  Result passes to next system — what is the interface?

Step 4: Completion
  Final state reached — how do you verify?
example.walkthrough: Apply the four-step anatomy method to Kotlin Core. Draw it as a flowing sequence, not a static diagram.

pitfalls: Treating Kotlin Core as an isolated component instead of part of a living flow
Skipping the dependency mapping — not asking 'what does this step need from the previous?'
Memorizing the steps without understanding WHY each one exists

Suggested daily loop:
  1. Complete 2-3 lessons (with knowledge checks)
  2. Work 3-5 scenarios in those domains
  3. Run 1 lab end-to-end
  4. 10 minutes of drills
example.walkthrough: The bootcamp mirrors how professionals actually work: learn the concept, apply it under realistic conditions, then prove it in the lab. Skipping straight to the mock without the lessons is the fastest way to fail it.

pitfalls: Skipping lessons and jumping to scenarios — the scenarios assume lesson knowledge
Treating the knowledge check as a formality instead of a real self-test
Ignoring the terminal and labs — hands-on reps are where durable skill comes from
lessons.try_it: Open the Learn path and complete the first lesson's knowledge check to see auto-completion in action.

lessons.title: interview Strategy: How to Win
concepts: The interview rewards applied understanding over memorization — every domain here maps to something you will actually be asked to do
Time management wins: in timed assessments, bank the easy wins first, flag the hard ones, and never leave a question blank
Wrong answers are data: each missed scenario reveals a specific gap. Log it, revisit the lesson, and re-attempt until the pattern clicks
Sleep and spacing beat cramming: 90-minute focused sessions with breaks outperform marathon sessions, especially the week before interview day

example.code:
The 3-pass method for timed assessments:
  Pass 1 (40% of time): answer everything you know cold
  Pass 2 (40% of time): work the flagged mediums with evidence
  Pass 3 (20% of time): educated guesses on the rest

Never spend 10 minutes on one question while five easy ones wait.
example.walkthrough: Elimination is a skill: practice ruling out two wrong choices fast, then deciding between the final two. Most scenario questions are designed so two options are clearly wrong to a prepared candidate.

pitfalls: Changing answers without new evidence — your first instinct after study is usually right
Perfectionism on one hard question while easy points expire
Studying new material the night before instead of reviewing what you know
lessons.try_it: Do one full timed mock this week using the 3-pass method, even before you feel ready. Baseline yourself.

lessons.title: Course Map: What You Will Master
concepts: This bootcamp has 15+ domains covering the full Android Interview landscape — from foundations to the capstone project
Core domains teach the must-know systems; the Systems Anatomy domain teaches you to see them as living, connected flows
The capstone project proves you can build and operate a real system end-to-end — this is your interview story
The mock assessment simulates the real interview so there are no surprises on the day

example.code:
Android Interview mastery map:
  Foundations -> Core systems (domains 2-10)
  -> Systems Anatomy (see it all connected)
  -> Capstone (build it yourself)
  -> Mock (prove it under pressure)
example.walkthrough: Start with: Kotlin Core. It unlocks everything downstream — the path is sequential for a reason.

pitfalls: Treating all domains as equal — weight your time toward the heaviest-tested areas
Skipping Systems Anatomy — it is the differentiator between passing and excelling
Saving the capstone for 'later' — start it early, iterate as you learn
lessons.try_it: Skim the domain list in the Learn path and note which three domains matter most for your goal. Start there after Start Here.

lessons.title: The Android Test Pyramid
concepts: The pyramid: many fast unit tests at the base, fewer integration tests in the middle, few slow UI tests at the top — invert it and your suite becomes slow, flaky, and expensive
Unit tests run on the JVM in the test/ source set with no emulator: ViewModels, use cases, mappers, validation logic should be nearly 100% covered here
Integration tests in androidTest/ verify components working together: Room DAOs against a real database, repository plus data source, navigation flows
UI tests with Espresso or Compose Test verify what the user sees and taps; keep them few, stable, and focused on critical journeys like login and checkout
Interview signal: when asked how you would test something, start with the pyramid — name what you unit test, what needs instrumentation, and what the UI test covers

example.walkthrough: Read the code top to bottom: the unit test builds the ViewModel with a fake repository — no network, no Android framework — and asserts the emitted state. It runs in milliseconds on the JVM. The comments show where the other layers live: Room DAO tests run on-device with an in-memory database, and a single Espresso test covers the tap-through journey.

pitfalls: Testing implementation details (private methods, exact call counts) instead of behavior — refactors then break tests that should have survived
One giant UI suite and no unit tests — the classic inverted pyramid: 20-minute runs, constant flakes, nobody trusts the suite
Network or time dependencies in unit tests — use fakes and TestDispatchers so tests are deterministic
lessons.try_it: Take one ViewModel from a sample app and list which behaviors are unit-testable on the JVM versus which need instrumentation. Write one unit test.

lessons.title: JUnit and Mockito-Style Unit Tests
concepts: AAA pattern — Arrange, Act, Assert — keeps every test readable: set up the fake, invoke the function, assert the outcome
Mock the boundaries, not the logic: mock repositories, clocks, and network clients; never mock the class under test or simple data classes
Test names are documentation: backtick names like `empty cart shows empty state` read as specifications
Parameterized tests cover input matrices — validation rules, mappers, formatters — without copy-paste
Coroutines in unit tests: runTest plus a TestDispatcher gives deterministic virtual time — no real delays

example.walkthrough: The test arranges a mocked repository returning an expired token, acts by calling ensureValidToken, and asserts the refreshed value. The mock/onBlocking/doReturn block is the Mockito-Kotlin DSL; runTest provides the coroutine scope. verify(repo).refresh() asserts the collaboration happened — use it sparingly and prefer asserting outcomes.

pitfalls: Over-verification: asserting every mock interaction makes tests brittle — verify outcomes first, interactions only when the interaction IS the requirement
Shared mutable state between tests (companion objects, singletons) — tests pass alone and fail together; use fresh instances per test
Forgetting runTest and TestDispatcher — real dispatchers make tests slow and flaky; always inject dispatchers
lessons.try_it: Write a unit test for a formatPrice utility using a parameterized test with five currency inputs.

lessons.title: UI Testing: Espresso and Compose Test
concepts: Espresso synchronizes with the main thread and IdlingResources automatically — flakiness usually means background work Espresso cannot see, like custom executors or raw threads
Compose Test uses semantics: onNodeWithText and onNodeWithTag — test what the user perceives, and add testTag only where text or content-description is insufficient
Test rules: ActivityScenarioRule launches the activity; createComposeRule gives you setContent for isolated composable tests
Keep UI tests hermetic: fake the repository layer so tests never hit a real network — a UI test failing because staging is down is a false failure
One assertion journey per test: login with valid credentials lands on home — not login plus settings plus logout in one mega-test

example.walkthrough: The rule creates a Compose test harness and setContent renders the screen with a fake ViewModel. The test asserts the button starts disabled, types an email via its test tag, then asserts the button enables. No emulator timing hacks — the Compose test framework synchronizes with recomposition automatically.

pitfalls: Thread.sleep in UI tests — the universal flakiness generator; rely on IdlingResources or the framework's own synchronization
Testing through real backends — hermetic fakes make UI tests fast and deterministic
Overly specific selectors (nested hierarchy matchers) — they break on every layout tweak; prefer text, content description, or a single testTag
lessons.try_it: Add a testTag to one input in a sample screen and write a Compose test that types text and asserts a button state change.

lessons.title: Testing Coroutines, Flow, and Fakes
concepts: TestDispatcher replaces real dispatchers: StandardTestDispatcher gives manual control via advanceUntilIdle — no real delays in tests
Turbine tests Flows fluently: flow.test { awaitItem(); awaitComplete() } asserts emissions in order, including errors
Fakes over mocks for repositories: a FakeUserRepository backed by a MutableStateFlow behaves like the real thing and is reusable across tests
The standard ViewModel pattern: create the ViewModel with a fake repo plus TestDispatcher, advanceUntilIdle, assert uiState — the interview answer
StandardTestDispatcher is the runTest default — deterministic and explicit; UnconfinedTestDispatcher executes eagerly and can hide ordering bugs

example.walkthrough: Turbine's test block subscribes to the StateFlow before the action — ordering matters. After triggering search and advancing the test scheduler, awaitItem asserts each emission in sequence: Loading, then Results. cancelAndIgnoreRemainingEvents cleans up the collector at the end.

pitfalls: Subscribing after the action — StateFlow replays the latest value, but a SharedFlow without replay drops emissions your test then misses
Real delay() in code under test without a TestDispatcher — tests take real seconds or time out
One fake per test file copy-pasted — put fakes in shared test fixtures so behavior stays consistent
lessons.try_it: Write a Turbine test for a ViewModel that debounces search input — assert only one emission for rapid successive queries.

lessons.title: Snapshot and Screenshot Testing
concepts: Screenshot tests catch unintended UI changes: render a composable or view, compare against a golden image, fail on pixel diffs
Paparazzi renders without a device — JVM-only screenshot tests that run in seconds on CI
Roborazzi runs on-device through the Compose test framework: real rendering, real fonts, real device configuration
Golden management: record goldens on one canonical configuration and review every diff deliberately — a changed golden is a decision, not an accident
Where they fit: above unit tests, below full UI journeys — component-level visual regression for design systems

example.walkthrough: Paparazzi renders the composable on the JVM and diffs against the recorded golden — no emulator, seconds on CI. Roborazzi captures from a real on-device Compose test, so fonts and rendering are faithful. Both fail on pixel differences; the workflow is record, review the diff deliberately, then accept or fix.

pitfalls: Auto-accepting golden changes — every diff is a UI change shipping to users; review them
Recording goldens on varying configs (font scale, dark mode) — diffs from environment, not code
Screenshot-testing whole screens for logic — keep goldens at component level; test behavior with semantics
lessons.try_it: Add Paparazzi to a sample module and record a golden for one button component in both light and dark theme.

lessons.title: Profiling with Android Studio
concepts: The profilers (CPU, Memory, Network, Energy) show what is actually happening — profile before optimizing, because intuition about bottlenecks is usually wrong
Always profile release-like builds: debug builds disable optimizations and inflate method counts, so debug timings mislead
CPU profiler: method tracing shows exact call counts and wall time — find the hot method, not the hot guess
Memory profiler: watch for a staircase allocation graph — memory that climbs and never returns signals a leak or unbounded cache
Baseline first: capture a before-trace so you can prove the fix worked with numbers, not feelings

example.walkthrough: Profiling is measurement, not vibes: record a fixed interaction (cold start, scroll a list, submit a form), note the numbers, change one thing, re-record. If you cannot reproduce the scenario identically, you cannot trust the comparison.

pitfalls: Optimizing without a baseline — you cannot prove the fix did anything
Profiling debug builds and acting on the numbers — ART behaves differently with optimizations on
Chasing micro-benchmarks while ignoring the 800ms network call on the main thread
lessons.try_it: Record a 10-second CPU trace of your app's cold start and list the top 3 methods by total time.

lessons.title: Smooth Rendering: Jank and Overdraw
concepts: The frame budget is 16.6ms at 60Hz: any frame that misses it is jank the user feels — Choreographer callbacks reveal exactly which frames skipped
Overdraw — pixels drawn multiple times per frame — is found with the GPU overdraw visualizer; flatten layouts and remove redundant backgrounds
RecyclerView jank usually comes from onBindViewHolder doing real work: image decoding, date formatting, string building — move it off the bind path or cache it
ConstraintLayout flattens deep view hierarchies; each nesting level multiplies measure/layout cost during scrolling
Baseline Profiles ship ahead-of-time compiled code paths for your critical journeys — cold start and first scroll get measurably faster

example.walkthrough: The GPU rendering bars turn jank from a feeling into a measurement: enable Profile GPU Rendering, scroll, and count bars crossing the green 16ms line. Then apply the RecyclerView fixes — setHasFixedSize, view cache, precomputed bind values — and re-measure. Fewer crossing bars is the proof.

pitfalls: Doing image loading or date parsing inside onBindViewHolder — the number one RecyclerView jank source
Deep LinearLayout nesting — 6+ levels makes every scroll frame pay measure/layout tax
Ignoring Baseline Profiles — free startup and scroll wins left on the table
lessons.try_it: Enable GPU overdraw visualization on a test device and screenshot your most complex screen. Identify the worst overdraw area.

lessons.title: Memory: Leaks, Bitmaps, and GC
concepts: The classic leak: a long-lived object holding an Activity context — static fields, singletons, and listeners registered but never unregistered
LeakCanary in debug builds detects retained Activity/Fragment instances automatically and shows the exact reference chain
Bitmaps are the big allocators: decode with inSampleSize matched to the ImageView size — a 4000px photo in a 200dp thumbnail wastes ~60x the memory
GC pauses cause jank: allocating in hot loops (onDraw, onBindViewHolder) triggers frequent collections — reuse objects with pools
onTrimMemory is your early warning: evict caches at TRIM_MEMORY_MODERATE before the system kills your process

example.walkthrough: The bitmap pattern is two-pass: first decode with inJustDecodeBounds to read dimensions without allocating, compute inSampleSize for the target view size, then decode for real. The context rule is simpler: statics and singletons get applicationContext or nothing — never an Activity.

pitfalls: Static field holding an Activity or View — survives rotation and leaks the whole view hierarchy
Loading full-resolution bitmaps into thumbnails — the most common OOM in image-heavy apps
Anonymous inner-class handlers/runnables capturing the outer Activity — use static inner classes with WeakReference or lifecycle-aware coroutines
lessons.try_it: Add LeakCanary to a sample app, rotate the device ten times on one screen, and read the leak report if one appears.

lessons.title: Startup Time and Battery
concepts: Cold start is measured to first frame: the Application.onCreate and first Activity inflation dominate — defer everything that is not needed for that first frame
Baseline Profiles plus Macrobenchmark give automated startup numbers in CI — track them like any other metric or they regress silently
Doze and App Standby defer background work: use WorkManager with constraints (charging, unmetered) instead of fighting the OS
AlarmManager exact alarms are restricted — prefer inexact alarms or WorkManager; exact alarms now need a special permission and Play review scrutiny
Battery Historian turns bug reports of drain into timelines: find the wake locks and network bursts your app actually caused

example.walkthrough: Two patterns: defer init until after the first frame with a Choreographer callback so cold start only pays for what the user sees, and schedule background sync with WorkManager constraints so the OS batches your work with the device's maintenance windows instead of waking the radio for you alone.

pitfalls: Initializing every SDK in Application.onCreate — analytics, crash reporting, and DI graphs all block first frame
Exact alarms or foreground services for periodic sync — Doze will defer you anyway; use WorkManager
Polling the network on a timer — push (FCM) or batched WorkManager jobs cost a fraction of the battery
lessons.try_it: List everything initialized in your Application.onCreate and mark each as first-frame-critical or deferrable. Defer one thing.

lessons.title: App Size and Install Optimization
concepts: Android App Bundle (AAB) is the upload format: Play generates optimized APKs per device — smaller downloads with no manual ABI splits
isMinifyEnabled plus isShrinkResources strip unused code and resources; check the APK Analyzer for what remains
Measure first: the top size offenders are usually native libraries, images, and bundled ML models — each gets a targeted fix
Dynamic Feature Modules defer delivery: ship the core now, download features on demand via Play Feature Delivery
Image discipline: WebP/AVIF over PNG, vector drawables for icons, density-specific resources only where vectors fail

example.walkthrough: The workflow is measure-then-cut: APK Analyzer ranks size contributors, and each gets a targeted fix — ABI filters for native libraries, WebP or vectors for images, dynamic features for rarely used screens. The AAB format means Play does per-device APK generation, so your job is shrinking the bundle, not hand-splitting APKs.

pitfalls: Uploading APKs instead of AABs — every user downloads every ABI and density
Shipping all ABIs (armeabi-v7a, arm64, x86_64) when nearly all devices are arm64-v8a
PNG screenshots and photos in drawable/ — the most common avoidable bloat
lessons.try_it: Run APK Analyzer on a sample APK and list the top 3 size contributors with a fix for each.

lessons.title: Sandbox, Permissions, and Intents
concepts: Every app runs as its own Linux UID in a sandbox: private files are private by default — security bugs come from what you explicitly expose
Runtime permissions (dangerous group: location, camera, microphone) must be requested in context and handle the user denying — including don't ask again
android:exported must be explicit on every component with an intent filter: an exported Activity or Service is an attack surface anyone can invoke
PendingIntents are capabilities: an implicit intent inside a PendingIntent lets the receiver fill in the target — use explicit intents
Deep links: verify App Links with assetlinks.json so no other app can claim your URLs; unclaimed deep links are hijackable

example.walkthrough: Two habits: ask for dangerous permissions at the moment of use with a rationale when the user previously denied, and default every component to exported=false unless it genuinely serves external callers. Most permission and intent vulnerabilities are defaults left unexamined.

pitfalls: Requesting all permissions at first launch — users deny what they do not understand; ask in context
Leaving android:exported=true on internal components — any app on the device can start them
Putting sensitive data in implicit intents or unprotected deep links — any app can intercept
lessons.try_it: Audit one app's manifest: list every exported component and justify each one in a sentence.

lessons.title: Secure Storage: Keystore and Encrypted Prefs
concepts: Never hardcode secrets: API keys in the APK are retrievable in minutes with apktool — keep secrets server-side or behind your own backend
Android Keystore holds cryptographic keys in hardware-backed storage: key material never enters your process memory in extractable form
EncryptedSharedPreferences encrypts both keys and values with a Keystore-backed master key — the right default for tokens and PII
EncryptedFile covers larger secrets; Room database encryption (SQLCipher) covers structured data at rest
Auto Backup includes SharedPreferences by default: exclude sensitive files with android:fullBackupContent rules or allowBackup=false for high-sensitivity apps

example.code:
// Tokens and PII: encrypted by default
val masterKey = MasterKey.Builder(ctx)
    .setKeyScheme(MasterKey.KeyScheme.AES256_GCM)
    .build()
val prefs = EncryptedSharedPreferences.create(
    ctx, "secrets", masterKey,
    EncryptedSharedPreferences.PrefKeyEncryptionScheme.AES256_SIV,
    EncryptedSharedPreferences.PrefValueEncryptionScheme.AES256_GCM
)
example.walkthrough: The pattern is one decision: anything sensitive goes through EncryptedSharedPreferences with a Keystore-backed master key — never plain SharedPreferences, never a hardcoded string. Then audit the backup rules so the encrypted file (and the key metadata) does not get swept into Auto Backup unexamined.

pitfalls: Hardcoding API keys or secrets in source or BuildConfig — the APK is not a safe
Rolling your own AES with a key in strings.xml — Keystore exists precisely so you do not manage key material
Storing refresh tokens in plain SharedPreferences — readable on any rooted device or via backup
lessons.try_it: Find every SharedPreferences usage in a sample app and classify each value as safe-plain or must-encrypt.

lessons.title: Network Security: TLS and Pinning
concepts: Cleartext HTTP is blocked by default (usesCleartextTraffic=false) — keep it that way; debug overrides belong in debug manifests only
The Network Security Config XML centralizes TLS policy: pin sets, debug CA trust, and per-domain rules in one reviewable file
Certificate pinning (OkHttp CertificatePinner) defeats MITM proxies even with a trusted CA — essential for banking, health, and auth endpoints
Pin with a backup pin and a rotation plan: a pin that expires with no update path bricks your app until users update
Validate hostnames and never disable hostname verification or trust-all TrustManagers — that Stack Overflow snippet is a vulnerability

example.code:
<!-- res/xml/network_security_config.xml -->
<network-security-config>
    <domain-config cleartextTrafficPermitted="false">
        <domain includeSubdomains="true">api.example.com</domain>
        <pin-set expiration="2027-01-01">
            <pin digest="SHA-256">base64==</pin>
            <pin digest="SHA-256">backup==</pin> <!-- rotation -->
        </pin-set>
    </domain-config>
</network-security-config>
example.walkthrough: The config declares the policy as data: no cleartext to the API domain, a pin set with an expiration date and a backup pin for rotation. Review it like code — the expiration date is a calendar item, and the backup pin is what saves you when the primary certificate rotates unexpectedly.

pitfalls: A trust-all X509TrustManager copied from a forum — disables all TLS validation app-wide
Pinning without a backup pin or rotation plan — certificate renewal becomes an outage
Debug CA certificates shipped in the release config — lets anyone with the debug CA proxy release traffic
lessons.try_it: Write a Network Security Config for a sample app: cleartext denied everywhere, debug CA trusted only in debug builds.

lessons.title: Hardening: Obfuscation and Anti-Tampering
concepts: R8 (minifyEnabled) shrinks and obfuscates release builds: smaller APK, renamed classes — a speed bump for reverse engineers, not a wall
Keep rules are the subtle art: too broad and nothing is obfuscated; too narrow and reflection/serialization breaks at runtime — test release builds
Play Integrity API attests the app is genuine and the device is trustworthy: gate sensitive actions (payments, rewards) on a passing verdict
Root detection is signal, not security: rooted devices can bypass client checks — enforce critical rules server-side and treat client signals as risk input
Tamper detection (signature verification at runtime) raises the bar for repackaged APKs; combine with server-side attestation for real assurance

example.walkthrough: Release builds flip three switches: minify, shrink resources, and your proguard rules. The discipline is testing the actual release artifact — install the release APK and exercise reflection-heavy paths (serialization, DI) because obfuscation breaks what debug builds never touch.

pitfalls: Shipping release builds unobfuscated — the APK is trivially decompilable as-is
Over-broad -keep rules that preserve everything — obfuscation in name only
Trusting client-side root/tamper checks as the security boundary — the server must enforce
lessons.try_it: Enable R8 on a sample app, build the release APK, and decompile one class before and after to see the difference.

lessons.title: Biometrics, OAuth, and App Links
concepts: BiometricPrompt is the system API for fingerprint and face: crypto-bound (CryptoObject) ties approval to a Keystore key so it cannot be replayed
OAuth on mobile uses Custom Tabs or the system browser with an App Links redirect — never a WebView, which can snoop credentials
App Links verified via assetlinks.json guarantee that only your app handles your OAuth redirect and deep links
PKCE (proof key for code exchange) secures the authorization code flow on public clients that cannot hold a client secret
Tokens: short-lived access tokens in EncryptedSharedPreferences, refreshed via the backend — never long-lived tokens on device

example.walkthrough: The biometric flow binds approval to a cryptographic operation: the Keystore key only unlocks inside the cipher the BiometricPrompt authorizes, so approval cannot be replayed elsewhere. OAuth goes through the system browser with an App Links redirect your assetlinks.json proves you own — the app never sees the password, and no other app can intercept the redirect.

pitfalls: WebView-based login — the app (or injected JS) can read credentials; use Custom Tabs
Biometric check as a boolean gate (if authenticated, proceed) — bypassable; bind to a CryptoObject
Unverified deep links for OAuth redirects — any app can claim them and steal the auth code
lessons.try_it: Verify an assetlinks.json for a sample domain and trace the OAuth redirect path from Custom Tab back into the app.

lessons.title: App Signing and Release Builds
concepts: Play App Signing is the standard: Google holds the app signing key, you hold the upload key — losing the upload key is recoverable, losing a self-managed app key is not
Build variants separate concerns: debug (debuggable, dev backend) vs release (minified, obfuscated, production backend) — never ship a debuggable build
The upload key signs the AAB you push to Play; Play re-signs with the app signing key for distribution — understand which key does what
Keep the keystore and its passwords in a secrets manager, not in the repo — a committed keystore is a compromised keystore
Test the actual release artifact: install the release AAB/APK locally and exercise reflection-heavy paths before uploading

example.walkthrough: The signing config reads everything from environment variables — nothing secret lives in version control. CI injects the keystore path and passwords at build time. This is the pattern interviewers expect: secrets flow from the secrets manager, never from the repo.

pitfalls: Committing the keystore or passwords to git — rotate immediately if this ever happens
Testing only debug builds and uploading release untested — obfuscation and shrinking break things debug never shows
Using the same key for upload and app signing manually — let Play App Signing hold the app key
lessons.try_it: Verify your release signing config reads all secrets from environment variables. List any secret still hardcoded.

lessons.title: Play Console Release Tracks
concepts: Tracks form a promotion pipeline: internal (fastest, up to 100 testers) -> closed -> open testing -> production — each stage widens the blast radius deliberately
Internal track is your smoke test: upload, install on real devices via the Play link, verify the release artifact before any wider audience
Closed tracks target specific tester lists (email groups) — ideal for beta communities and client review builds
Open testing is public-but-labeled: anyone can join, the listing shows it is a test version — real-world diversity without production risk
Promote, do not re-upload: promoting the same tested artifact up the tracks guarantees production runs exactly what testers ran

example.code:
Release pipeline:
  1. Upload AAB to internal track -> install on 3 real devices
  2. Promote to closed track -> beta group tests for 3 days
  3. Promote to production at 10% staged rollout
  4. Monitor crash/ANR for 48h -> resume to 100%
Same artifact, widening audience, metrics gate each step.
example.walkthrough: The discipline is promotion of one artifact through widening rings, with metrics gating each promotion. Re-uploading a fresh build to production skips every test the earlier tracks performed — the pipeline only works if the artifact is identical.

pitfalls: Uploading straight to production — no track has validated the artifact
Rebuilding between tracks — the tested artifact is not the shipped artifact
Skipping the internal-track install check — the cheapest verification, skipped most often
lessons.try_it: Write the track-promotion checklist you would follow for your next release, with the metric gate at each step.

lessons.title: Versioning and Updates
concepts: versionCode is the integer Play uses to order releases — it must increase with every upload; versionName is the human string users see
Semantic versioning (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH) communicates change magnitude: breaking changes bump MAJOR, features bump MINOR, fixes bump PATCH
The In-App Updates API offers flexible (background download, user continues) vs immediate (blocking, for critical fixes) flows — use Play's mechanism, not a custom updater
Stale-app strategy: gate critical features on a minimum versionCode server-side so ancient clients cannot hit deprecated endpoints
versionCode mistakes are permanent: uploading versionCode 42 after 43 was live means 42 can never ship — plan the numbering

example.walkthrough: versionCode 47 orders this release after 46 — Play rejects anything lower. The in-app update call starts Play's own update flow; FLEXIBLE downloads in the background for routine updates while IMMEDIATE blocks for must-have fixes. Never build a custom APK downloader — Play's flow handles signatures and verification.

pitfalls: Decreasing or reusing versionCode — Play rejects the upload and the number is burned
Custom in-app updaters downloading APKs — bypasses Play signature verification and scares users
No minimum-version gating — five-year-old clients hitting retired APIs generate phantom bug reports
lessons.try_it: Check your versionCode history: confirm it strictly increases and document the scheme for the next three planned releases.

lessons.title: Pre-Launch Report and Rollout Safety
concepts: The pre-launch report runs your app on real devices in Firebase Test Lab automatically: crashes, ANRs, screenshots, and accessibility issues before users see anything
Read it like a release gate: new crashes or security warnings block promotion — it exists to catch what your test lab missed
Staged rollouts limit blast radius: start at 10%, watch crash/ANR rates for 24-48h, then resume — halt at the first anomaly
Define halt criteria in advance: crash rate above X%, a new crash cluster, ANR spike — deciding the threshold mid-incident is how bad rollouts continue
Rollout halt is one click in Play Console — rehearse finding it before you need it at 2 AM

example.code:
Rollout runbook:
  HALT if: crash-free rate drops >0.5% vs baseline,
    or any new crash cluster appears in the top 5,
    or ANR rate exceeds 0.8%.
  On halt: pause rollout in Play Console, pull the
  stack traces, fix, and roll a new release — never
  resume a halted rollout without a fix.
example.walkthrough: Write the halt criteria before the rollout starts, when you are calm and rational. During the incident you will be tempted to wait one more hour — the pre-written threshold makes the halt decision automatic instead of emotional.

pitfalls: Ignoring the pre-launch report — automated device testing you already paid for with the upload
100% day-one rollouts — maximum blast radius for every bug you missed
No halt criteria — every anomaly becomes a debate instead of a decision
lessons.try_it: Open your last pre-launch report (or a sample) and list the top 3 findings you would gate a release on.

lessons.title: Play Policies and Store Listing
concepts: Target API requirements: Play mandates a recent targetSdkVersion for new and updated apps — missing the deadline blocks releases entirely
Data safety section: you must declare data collection, sharing, and security practices — it must match your privacy policy and actual behavior
Permissions declarations: sensitive permissions (background location, accessibility) need a Play Console declaration with a video demo of the feature
Store listing: the icon, feature graphic, and first screenshots decide installs — A/B test with store listing experiments
Policy strikes accumulate: repeated violations can suspend the app or terminate the developer account — treat policy review as part of definition of done

example.walkthrough: Run the checklist before every release, not after a rejection: the target API level gates your ability to ship at all, the data safety form is a legal attestation that must match reality, and sensitive permissions need declarations with video evidence. Store listing assets are your conversion funnel — experiment, do not guess.

pitfalls: Discovering the target API deadline on release day — track Play's annual requirement calendar
Data safety form copied from a template that does not match your SDKs' actual data collection
Requesting background location just in case — declarations get rejected and the release stalls
lessons.try_it: Fill a draft Data safety section for a sample app and cross-check each answer against its actual SDK list.

lessons.title: Capstone: Offline-First Task Manager — Overview
concepts: Your capstone: a production-quality offline-first Android app with a full test pyramid, performance budgets, hardened security, and a Play-ready signed release
Break the build into phases: plan, build, secure, validate, document. Each phase maps to domains in this bootcamp
Document as you go — your write-up is the interview artifact that proves senior-level ownership
Done beats perfect: a working system with honest limitations beats an unfinished ambitious one

example.code:
Phase 1: Plan the data layer: Room database, repository, WorkManager sync
Phase 2: Build the UI in Compose with a full test pyramid (unit, integration, UI)
Phase 3: Profile and fix performance: startup time, scroll jank, memory
Phase 4: Harden security: encrypted storage, certificate pinning, R8 obfuscation
Phase 5: Cut a signed release build and rehearse the Play track rollout
example.walkthrough: Treat each phase as a mini-project with a definition of done. Demo each phase working before moving on — integration surprises compound.

pitfalls: Starting to build before writing the plan — an hour of planning saves ten of rework
Skipping documentation until the end — you will forget why decisions were made
Gold-plating phase one while phase four remains untouched
lessons.try_it: Write the one-paragraph project plan: what you will build, in what phases, and what 'done' looks like.

lessons.title: Capstone: Validation and Demo
concepts: Validate every requirement with a test you can show: screenshots, command output, or a live demo
Prepare the 5-minute demo narrative: problem, approach, build, validation, lessons learned
Anticipate questions: know the trade-offs you made and what you would do with more time
Publish the write-up: architecture diagram, build log, validation evidence, reflection

example.code:
Demo script template:
  1. The problem (30s)
  2. Architecture overview (60s)
  3. Live walkthrough (2 min)
  4. Validation evidence (60s)
  5. What I would do next (30s)
example.walkthrough: A demo that only shows the happy path invites the hardest questions. Show one failure mode and how the system handles it — that is what interviewers remember.

pitfalls: Demoing without rehearsing — run it three times end-to-end first
Hiding limitations — name them before you are asked
No architecture diagram — draw the system before you demo it
lessons.try_it: Draft your 5-minute demo script for the capstone project.

lessons.title: Null Safety: Ending the Billion-Dollar Mistake
concepts: Kotlin's type system distinguishes nullable (String?) from non-null (String) at compile time — the NPE moves from runtime crash to compile error
Safe call (?.), Elvis (?:), and non-null assertion (!!) — prefer the first two; !! is a code smell that reintroduces the crash
let with safe calls: user?.let { ... } executes the block only when non-null
Platform types (String!) from Java interop: the compiler cannot guarantee nullability — treat every Java return as suspect and null-check at the boundary
lateinit vs nullable var vs lazy: choose by lifecycle — lateinit for injected fields, lazy for expensive computed values, nullable for genuinely absent state

example.walkthrough: The greet function shows the idiom: safe call plus Elvis collapses null handling into one expression with no branches. The Java interop line is the interview trap — getString returns a platform type, so the Elvis with error() converts the uncertainty into an explicit decision at the boundary instead of a crash three screens later.

pitfalls: !! scattered through the codebase — every one is a deferred crash; replace with explicit handling
Trusting platform types from Java — null-check at the boundary, not deep in business logic
Overusing nullable vars for state that has a real default — prefer non-null with a sensible initial value
lessons.try_it: Find three !! operators in a sample codebase and rewrite each with safe-call/Elvis or an explicit error.

lessons.title: Data Classes, Sealed Classes, and Plain Classes
concepts: Data classes auto-generate equals, hashCode, toString, copy — use them for value holders (DTOs, UI state snapshots); a plain class is for behavior and identity
Sealed classes restrict hierarchies to known subtypes: the compiler enforces exhaustive when — the standard for UI state (Loading, Success, Error)
Sealed interface vs sealed class vs enum: interface for multi-inheritance flexibility, class for shared state, enum when cases carry no data
copy() enables immutable state updates: state.copy(isLoading = false) — the foundation of UDF in ViewModels
Destructuring and componentN come free with data classes — convenient, but do not destructure across module boundaries where field order is a hidden contract

example.walkthrough: The sealed interface models every possible UI state as a type, and the when expression is compiler-checked exhaustive — add a new subtype and every when breaks until handled. That is the whole point: impossible states become unrepresentable, and the compiler finds the places you forgot.

pitfalls: Stringly-typed state (status: String = 'loading') — typos become runtime bugs; sealed hierarchies make them compile errors
Data class with mutable vars — copy() on mutable state defeats immutability; use val
Sealed class with dozens of subtypes — a sign the state model needs splitting, not extending
lessons.try_it: Convert a string-status field in a sample ViewModel to a sealed UI state and fix every when to be exhaustive.

lessons.title: Extension Functions and Scope Functions
concepts: Extension functions add behavior without inheritance: fun String.isEmail(): Boolean — resolved statically, so they cannot override and should not fake polymorphism
Member functions win over extensions on signature clash — extensions are syntactic sugar, not virtual dispatch
Scope functions: let (null-check plus transform), run (compute with receiver), with (operate on non-null), apply (configure and return receiver), also (side effects, return receiver)
apply for builders, also for logging and telemetry side effects, let for nullable chains — using the wrong one obscures intent
Interview trap: extension on a nullable receiver (fun String?.safe()) is legal and often the cleanest null-handling idiom

example.walkthrough: Each scope function answers a different question: apply configures and returns the receiver, also performs a side effect and returns the receiver, let transforms (often a nullable) and returns the lambda result. Picking by intent makes the code self-documenting — a reader knows apply means configuration without reading the body.

pitfalls: Nesting scope functions 4 deep — the receiver/it confusion becomes unreadable; extract a named function
Extension functions that should be members — if it needs private state, it belongs inside the class
Shadowing: an extension named like a member misleads readers into expecting virtual dispatch
lessons.try_it: Rewrite a 5-line null-check-and-configure block using let and apply, then compare readability.

lessons.title: Delegation: Composition in One Keyword
concepts: by delegates interface implementation to a composed object: class Repo(api: Api) : Api by api — composition without boilerplate
lazy: thread-safe deferred initialization — val config by lazy { loadConfig() } — computed once, on first access
observable/vetoable: Delegates.observable fires a callback on change — lightweight reactive state without Flow
Custom delegates via getValue/setValue operators: build once (for example a preference-backed delegate) and reuse everywhere
Class delegation vs inheritance: prefer by-composition for behavior reuse; inheritance is for true is-a relationships

example.walkthrough: CachedRepo delegates the entire Api interface to the wrapped api in one keyword, then overrides only get() to add caching — all other methods forward automatically. The property delegates show the two workhorses: lazy defers expensive reads until needed, observable turns a var into a change-notifier without ceremony.

pitfalls: Delegating then overriding everything — if you override all methods, you did not need delegation
lazy with side effects and NONE mode in multi-threaded code — the default SYNCHRONIZED mode is safe
observable triggering heavy work (network) on every keystroke — debounce before acting
lessons.try_it: Write a preference-backed delegate: var username by prefs.string("username", "") backed by SharedPreferences.

lessons.title: Reified Generics and Inline Functions
concepts: Type erasure: at runtime List<String> is just List — generic type arguments do not survive, so you cannot do arg is T
reified with inline: inline fun <reified T> parse(json: String): T — the compiler substitutes the real type at each call site
Use cases: type-safe intent extras, JSON parsing, startActivity<T>() helpers — anywhere you would otherwise pass Class<T>
inline also enables non-local returns and avoids lambda allocation overhead in hot paths
Cost: inlining duplicates bytecode at every call site — use for small functions and reified needs, not giant utilities

example.walkthrough: The reified version erases the Class parameter from the call site — the compiler inlines the actual type, so T::class.java works. Compare the two signatures: the non-reified one forces every caller to pass String::class.java, the reified one reads like a normal generic function. That call-site cleanliness is why every Android codebase has a reified arg()/fromJson() helper.

pitfalls: reified without inline — does not compile; reified requires inlining
Inlining large functions called from many sites — bytecode bloat; keep inlined functions small
Using reified where a simple overload would do — do not pay inlining costs for marginal syntax wins
lessons.try_it: Write an inline reified startActivity<T : Activity>() extension on Context and use it to launch an activity.

lessons.title: Activity and Fragment Lifecycles
concepts: Activity order: onCreate -> onStart -> onResume -> onPause -> onStop -> onDestroy; onRestart sits between onStop and onStart on return
onCreate is for one-time setup (setContentView, ViewModel init); onResume/onPause bracket interactivity (camera, sensors, animations)
Fragment adds onAttach/onCreateView/onViewCreated/onDestroyView — the view lifecycle is shorter than the fragment lifecycle, the number one source of view-binding leaks
Clear view bindings in onDestroyView, not onDestroy — the fragment instance can outlive its view across back-stack operations
Modern guidance: single-Activity architecture with the Navigation component — Activities become entry points, Fragments (or Compose destinations) become screens

example.walkthrough: The binding pattern exists because of the lifecycle mismatch: the fragment can sit on the back stack with no view. Nulling _binding in onDestroyView releases the entire view hierarchy; holding it until onDestroy leaks every view through every back-stack stay. The !! on the getter is the one acceptable use — it fails fast during the valid window.

pitfalls: Accessing binding after onDestroyView — the classic back-stack crash; null it and guard
Heavy work in onCreate of every Activity — startup cost multiplies per entry point
Registering listeners in onResume but unregistering in onDestroy — asymmetric pairing leaks across pause/resume cycles
lessons.try_it: Add lifecycle logging to each callback of a sample Activity, then rotate and background the app and narrate the log.

lessons.title: Intents: Explicit, Implicit, and Deep Links
concepts: Explicit intents name the component (Intent(this, DetailActivity::class.java)) — intra-app navigation, no resolution needed
Implicit intents declare an action (ACTION_VIEW, ACTION_SEND) — the system resolves handlers; any app can claim them
Intent filters advertise capabilities in the manifest; android:exported must be explicit on every filtered component
Deep links route URLs into screens; App Links (verified via assetlinks.json) prove ownership so no other app can hijack your URLs
Extras are untyped: define const val keys and document types — a mismatched getStringExtra returns null silently

example.walkthrough: Explicit intents are for your own components — direct and safe. The intent-filter with autoVerify turns a deep link into an App Link: Android checks assetlinks.json on your domain, and only your app opens those URLs. Without verification it is a plain deep link any app can claim, which is both a UX and a security problem.

pitfalls: Implicit intents for internal navigation — any app can intercept; use explicit internally
autoVerify without a valid assetlinks.json — verification silently fails and links open in the browser
Reading extras without defaults — getIntExtra without a default masks missing data as 0
lessons.try_it: Add an App Link intent-filter to a sample app and verify assetlinks.json serves with content-type application/json.

lessons.title: Fragments: Transactions and State Loss
concepts: FragmentManager transactions are async: commit() schedules, executePendingTransactions() forces — state loss happens when you commit after onSaveInstanceState
IllegalStateException: Can not perform this action after onSaveInstanceState — the framework cannot guarantee the transaction survives process death
Fixes: commit before state save, use commitAllowingStateLoss only when the UI state is truly disposable, or post the transaction to the next lifecycle event
Back stack: addToBackStack() makes Back reverse the transaction; without it, Back exits — a UX decision per screen
Modern alternative: the Navigation component manages transactions, back stack, and deep links declaratively — fewer hand-written transactions, fewer state-loss bugs

example.walkthrough: The guard is the lesson: async callbacks (network responses, timers) fire whenever they want, including after the framework saved state. Checking isStateSaved before committing — and deferring to onResume when set — eliminates the crash class entirely instead of suppressing it with commitAllowingStateLoss.

pitfalls: commitAllowingStateLoss as a habit — it hides the bug; the transaction can still vanish after process death
Committing transactions from background threads — FragmentManager is main-thread only
Nested fragments with getFragmentManager instead of childFragmentManager — transactions target the wrong manager
lessons.try_it: Trigger a state-loss crash deliberately (commit in a delayed callback after backgrounding), then fix it with the isStateSaved guard.

lessons.title: RecyclerView Internals
concepts: ViewHolder pattern: views are inflated once and recycled — onCreateViewHolder is rare, onBindViewHolder is constant; expensive work belongs in the former
Recycling means stale state: every bind must set every visible property — a recycled view remembers the last item's data
DiffUtil computes minimal updates (insert/move/remove) off the main thread — no more notifyDataSetChanged jank and free item animations
ListAdapter plus DiffUtil.ItemCallback is the modern default: submitList() diffs on a background thread and animates changes
View types: getItemViewType for heterogeneous lists — each type gets its own ViewHolder pool; misused types cause ClassCastException on recycle

example.walkthrough: ListAdapter handles the diffing: submitList posts the new list, DiffUtil compares on a background thread using your areItemsTheSame/areContentsTheSame, and only changed rows rebind with animations. The bind comment is the eternal rule — recycled views carry the previous item's state, so bind must be total, not incremental.

pitfalls: notifyDataSetChanged on every update — kills animations and rebinds everything; use DiffUtil
Partial binds (setting text but not image) — recycled views show the wrong image from the previous item
areItemsTheSame comparing full objects — defeats move detection; compare stable IDs
lessons.try_it: Convert a notifyDataSetChanged adapter to ListAdapter and watch the item animations appear.

lessons.title: Configuration Changes and State Survival
concepts: Rotation destroys and recreates the Activity by default — the framework calls onSaveInstanceState, then rebuilds
ViewModel survives configuration changes (scoped to the Activity/Fragment lifecycle) — UI state and in-flight work live here, not in the Activity
onSaveInstanceState Bundle: for transient UI state (scroll position, form input) that must survive process death too — keep it small and parcelable
rememberSaveable in Compose: the equivalent — survives both rotation and process death via the saved instance state registry
What ViewModel does NOT survive: process death — persist critical state to DataStore or Room; ViewModel is for config changes, storage is for death

example.walkthrough: Two survival tiers: ViewModel and mutableStateOf survive rotation because the ViewModelStore outlives the Activity instance; rememberSaveable goes further by writing to the saved-state registry, surviving process death. The interview answer names both tiers and their limits — and notes that anything the user must never lose goes to disk.

pitfalls: Storing everything in onSaveInstanceState — Bundles are small and slow; large data belongs in the ViewModel or storage
Assuming ViewModel survives process death — it does not; test with Don't keep activities plus backgrounding
remember without Saveable for form input — rotation wipes the form and users notice
lessons.try_it: Enable Don't keep activities, background your app mid-form, return, and verify which state survived and which did not.

lessons.title: Suspend Functions and Structured Concurrency
concepts: suspend marks a function that can pause without blocking a thread — sequential-looking code that does not hold threads hostage
Structured concurrency: every coroutine runs in a scope; when the scope dies, its children are cancelled — no leaked background work
launch (fire-and-forget Job) vs async (Deferred with a result) — use async only when you need the return value; await() propagates exceptions
CoroutineScope hierarchy: viewModelScope and lifecycleScope tie coroutines to UI lifecycles — the default choice for UI work
Never use GlobalScope in app code — unstructured, uncancelled, untestable

example.walkthrough: The two async blocks run concurrently inside the viewModelScope; await() collects both results, and if either throws, the other cancels — structured concurrency in action.
