The loadFeed function looks synchronous but suspends at each call, freeing the thread. Contrast with callbacks: same concurrency, a tenth of the nesting.

pitfalls: GlobalScope.launch for UI work — survives the screen, leaks, and cannot be cancelled coherently
async without await — exceptions vanish silently until the Deferred is GC'd
Blocking calls (Thread.sleep, .get()) inside coroutines — defeats the entire purpose; use suspend equivalents
lessons.try_it: Convert a callback-based repository method to a suspend function and call it from viewModelScope.

lessons.title: Dispatchers: Main, IO, and Default
concepts: Dispatchers.Main: the UI thread — updating views and state; Main.immediate avoids a dispatch when already on Main
Dispatchers.IO: blocking I/O (disk, network blocking calls) — a large thread pool built for blocking
Dispatchers.Default: CPU-intensive work (sorting, parsing, image processing) — sized to CPU cores
withContext switches dispatcher mid-coroutine: withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { db.query() } — cheap, structured, no callbacks
Room and Retrofit suspend functions handle their own threading — do not wrap them in withContext(IO); that is the library's job

example.walkthrough: The withContext block moves only the CPU-heavy parse to Default; the suspend repo call was already main-safe. Control returns to the caller's dispatcher (Main, from viewModelScope) after the block, so the state update needs no manual thread hop. The rule: switch dispatchers for the work, not for the call.

pitfalls: withContext(Dispatchers.IO) around Retrofit suspend calls — redundant; the library already dispatches
Updating UI state from Dispatchers.Default — state writes must happen on Main
Dispatchers.IO for CPU-bound loops — starves the IO pool meant for blocking calls
lessons.try_it: Audit one repository: remove redundant withContext(IO) wrappers around suspend DAO/Retrofit calls.

lessons.title: Exception Handling and Supervision
concepts: A child exception cancels the parent scope and all siblings by default — one failed request kills the whole screen's work
supervisorScope: children fail independently — use when requests are independent (feed plus notifications plus profile)
SupervisorJob in a custom scope gives the same isolation for long-lived scopes
CoroutineExceptionHandler catches uncaught exceptions from launch (not async — async holds them until await)
Result<T> and runCatching as return values: for per-item resilience where exceptions are data, not crashes

example.walkthrough: Inside supervisorScope, the feed and notification requests are independent: if notifications fail, the feed still renders. runCatching converts the notification failure into a default empty list — the screen degrades gracefully instead of dying. Without supervisorScope, the notification exception would cancel the feed request too.

pitfalls: Catching Exception around the whole scope — masks cancellation; never swallow CancellationException
CoroutineExceptionHandler on async — it never fires there; exceptions surface at await()
supervisorScope for dependent requests — if B needs A's result, they are not independent; let failure propagate
lessons.try_it: Wrap two independent loads in supervisorScope and verify one failing still renders the other.

lessons.title: StateFlow vs SharedFlow
concepts: StateFlow: holds a value, replays the latest to new collectors — the UI state holder; always has a value (needs an initial)
SharedFlow: no value, configurable replay — the event bus; emits events (navigation, toasts, snackbars)
The event problem: StateFlow replays, so a navigate state retriggers on rotation — one-shot events belong in SharedFlow (replay=0) or a Channel
Sharing strategies: shareIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5000), replay=1) turns a cold flow hot for the UI
stateIn converts any Flow to StateFlow — the standard repository-to-ViewModel bridge

example.walkthrough: Two flows, two jobs: uiState is a StateFlow with Loading as the initial value — collectors always get the current screen state, surviving rotation. _events is a SharedFlow with no replay — a snackbar event emitted while nobody collects is dropped, which is correct for events but would be a bug for state. Mixing them up causes the classic bugs: replayed navigation and lost UI state.

pitfalls: One-shot events in StateFlow — rotation replays the navigation event and the user teleports
SharedFlow for UI state — new collectors (post-rotation) get nothing until the next emission
SharingStarted.Eagerly in ViewModels — starts work with no collectors; WhileSubscribed(5000) survives quick rotations
lessons.try_it: Convert a LiveData event wrapper (SingleLiveEvent) to SharedFlow and delete the wrapper class.

lessons.title: Debounce, Retry, and Flow Patterns
concepts: debounce(300): wait for a pause in emissions — the search-as-you-type pattern; only the settled query hits the network
flatMapLatest: switch to the newest query's flow, cancelling the previous — stale results can never overwrite fresh ones
retryWhen with exponential backoff: transient failures (timeout) retry, permanent ones (401) do not — inspect the exception
combine vs zip: combine emits on any upstream change (search query plus filters), zip pairs emissions one-to-one
cancellable(): mark cleanup points in non-cancellable sections so cancellation still propagates

example.code:
// Search-as-you-type: the canonical Flow pipeline
val results: StateFlow<List<Item>> = query
    .debounce(300)                          // wait for typing pause
    .filter { it.length >= 2 }               // ignore stubs
    .flatMapLatest { repo.search(it) }       // cancel stale requests
    .retryWhen { cause, attempt ->
        cause is IOException && attempt < 3   // transient only
    }
    .stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5000), emptyList())
example.walkthrough: Read the pipeline as a sentence: queries debounce 300ms, short stubs are filtered, each settled query switches to a fresh search (cancelling the in-flight one), IO failures retry up to 3 times, and the whole thing becomes UI state. flatMapLatest is the key insight — without it, a slow first query overwrites the fast second one.

pitfalls: debounce on the result instead of the query — debouncing results delays rendering, not requests
Retrying 401s — auth failures need re-login, not retries; retry only transient errors
flatMapConcat for search — queues stale requests instead of cancelling them
lessons.try_it: Build the search pipeline above against a fake repository with artificial delays and verify stale results never win.

lessons.title: DataStore Over SharedPreferences
concepts: SharedPreferences is synchronous, untyped, and error-swallowing (apply() failures are silent) — DataStore is its async, typed replacement
Preferences DataStore: key-value storage like SharedPreferences but with Flow reads and transactional writes
Proto DataStore: typed schema with Protocol Buffers — compile-time safety for settings objects
Migration path: DataStore supports SharedPreferencesMigration — migrate once, delete the old file, never look back
What DataStore is NOT: a database — lists, relations, and queries belong in Room

example.walkthrough: Reads become Flows — the token is observed, not polled — and writes are suspending transactions that commit fully or not at all. The migration line is the practical bridge: existing users' SharedPreferences move over on first launch, and the old API can be deleted. New code should never touch SharedPreferences.

pitfalls: Using DataStore for relational data — it is key-value; reach for Room at the first sign of queries
Blocking reads (runBlocking { dataStore.data.first() }) on the main thread — collect the Flow instead
Storing large blobs in DataStore — the whole file is read on access; blobs belong in files with Room metadata
lessons.try_it: Migrate one SharedPreferences usage to Preferences DataStore and observe the value as a Flow.

lessons.title: Room: Entities, DAOs, and Relations
concepts: Entity = table: @Entity data class with @PrimaryKey; DAOs declare @Query/@Insert/@Update/@Delete — Room generates the implementation at compile time
Suspend DAO functions are main-safe — Room dispatches automatically; Flow-returning queries emit on every table change
Relations: @Relation for one-to-many, @Embedded for flattening — model the object graph, not just tables
@Transaction on multi-query methods — without it, a relation query can read a half-updated database
TypeConverters bridge custom types (Date, enums, lists) — keep converters small and total

example.walkthrough: The DAO is the contract: observeAll returns a Flow that re-emits whenever the post table changes — the UI just collects. upsertAll is a suspend function, main-safe by Room. The @Transaction annotation on the relation query is the subtle correctness point: the post and its comments are read atomically, never a torn view.

pitfalls: Queries on the main thread with allowMainThreadQueries in production — it is a debug escape hatch, not a strategy
Missing @Transaction on relation reads — inconsistent object graphs under concurrent writes
DAOs returning LiveData in new code — Flow is the modern default
lessons.try_it: Write a @Relation query for posts-with-comments and verify it emits updates when a comment is inserted.

lessons.title: Room Migrations
concepts: Schema changes need Migration objects: Migration(1, 2) with ALTER TABLE — Room validates the resulting schema against your entities
Destructive fallback (fallbackToDestructiveMigration) wipes user data — acceptable in dev, a data-loss bug in production
Auto-migrations (@AutoMigration(from=1, to=2)) handle additive changes like new tables or columns without handwritten SQL
Test migrations with room-testing: create the old schema, insert data, migrate, assert the data survived — the highest-value DB test
Export schemas (exportSchema=true): the JSON history lets Room validate and lets you test any version jump

example.walkthrough: The migration adds a non-null column with a default — the DEFAULT 0 is what keeps existing rows valid. The test is the real lesson: create version 1, insert a row, run the migration with validation, and assert the data survived. Untested migrations are the top cause of upgrade crashes.

pitfalls: NOT NULL column without DEFAULT — migration crashes on existing rows
Skipping exportSchema — you lose the ability to test migrations against real history
Renaming a table by drop and create — data loss; use ALTER TABLE ... RENAME TO
lessons.try_it: Add a column to a sample entity, write the Migration, and test it with room-testing.

lessons.title: MediaStore and Scoped Storage
concepts: Since Android 10, scoped storage: apps see only their own files plus media via MediaStore — broad external-storage access is gone
Saving a photo: insert into MediaStore.Images with IS_PENDING=1, write the bytes, then clear IS_PENDING — the gallery sees it only when complete
No storage permission needed to write your own media via MediaStore; READ_MEDIA_IMAGES (Android 13+) reads other apps' media
App-specific storage (getExternalFilesDir) needs no permissions at all — deleted with the app, invisible to galleries
requestLegacyExternalStorage is dead — code written for it breaks on modern Android; migrate to the MediaStore flow

example.walkthrough: The IS_PENDING dance is the protocol: mark the entry pending, write the bytes, then unmark — other apps never see a half-written file. This replaced the old write-anywhere model. Note no permission request for your own media: scoped storage made the common case permission-free.

pitfalls: Writing to arbitrary external paths — fails on Android 10 and above; use MediaStore or app-specific dirs
Forgetting IS_PENDING — gallery apps may read partial files
Requesting MANAGE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE for a gallery feature — Play rejects it; use the media permissions
lessons.try_it: Save a generated bitmap via MediaStore and confirm it appears in the device gallery.

lessons.title: Offline-First Sync and Choosing the Store
concepts: Offline-first: the local database (Room) is the source of truth the UI reads; the network syncs it in the background via WorkManager
Sync direction matters: pull (server to device, straightforward) vs push (device to server, needs conflict resolution)
Conflict strategies: last-write-wins (simple, lossy), server-wins, client-wins, or field-level merge — choose per entity and document it
Sync metadata: serverVersion/updatedAt per row plus a sync status flag (SYNCED, PENDING, FAILED) drives retry and UI badges
Choosing the store: DataStore for settings and flags, Room for structured queryable data, files plus Room metadata for blobs, MediaStore for shared media

example.walkthrough: The worker is the sync engine: pull changes since the last sync, apply them in a transaction, push local pending changes, mark them synced, and advance the watermark. IOException retries via WorkManager backoff; anything else fails loudly. The UI never talks to the network — it observes Room, which the worker keeps fresh.

pitfalls: UI reading the network directly with a Room cache for offline — two sources of truth that disagree
No sync status flags — the user cannot tell what is uploaded and support cannot debug it
Syncing on every app start without constraints — battery and data drain; use WorkManager constraints
lessons.try_it: Add a syncStatus column to one entity and show a pending-upload badge in its list row.

lessons.title: MVVM and the ViewModel
concepts: MVVM on Android: the View (Activity/Compose) observes ViewModel state; the ViewModel holds UI state and logic; the Model (repository) owns data
ViewModel survives configuration changes via ViewModelStore — the reason UI state does not live in the Activity
No Android framework references in the ViewModel (no Context, no Views) — keeps it unit-testable on the JVM
Expose immutable StateFlow publicly, mutate a private MutableStateFlow internally — the state encapsulation contract
ViewModel is UI-scoped: business logic reusable across screens belongs in use cases, not the ViewModel

example.walkthrough: The pattern in miniature: private mutable state, public immutable flow, one entry point driving Loading to Success or Error. The ViewModel knows nothing about Activities or Composables — it produces state, the UI renders it. That separation is what makes the whole class unit-testable with a fake AuthRepo.

pitfalls: Context or View references in the ViewModel — leaks and untestable; pass only what you need
Multiple mutable states updated independently — inconsistent intermediate states; prefer a single UI state object
Business logic duplicated across ViewModels — extract use cases when the second screen needs it
lessons.try_it: Refactor a ViewModel that holds a Context to take only the needed repository instead.

lessons.title: The Repository Pattern
concepts: Repository = single source of truth: the UI asks the repository; the repository decides network vs cache vs database
Abstract data sources behind interfaces: NetworkDataSource, LocalDataSource — the repository orchestrates, sources implement
Expose Flows from the repository: the UI collects and reacts — no manual refresh calls scattered through the UI
Repository per aggregate (UserRepository, FeedRepository), not per table — align with domain concepts, not database schema
Where it lives: the data layer module; the UI layer depends on the repository interface, never on Retrofit or Room directly

example.walkthrough: The UI collects observeFeed and gets cached data immediately; onStart triggers a refresh that writes through the single write path into Room, which re-emits. The UI never knows about the network — it sees one Flow of truth. That is the entire pattern: orchestrate sources, expose one stream.

pitfalls: Repository returning network Flows directly — no offline story, no single source of truth
UI calling api and dao separately — orchestration logic leaks into the View layer
God repository (AppRepository) — split by aggregate before it becomes unmaintainable
lessons.try_it: Draw your app's data flow: UI to repository to sources. Circle every place the UI touches a source directly and fix one.

lessons.title: Unidirectional Data Flow with Compose
concepts: UDF: state flows down, events flow up — the composable renders state and reports user actions; it never mutates shared state directly
State hoisting: move state to the lowest common owner — hoist until the state is shared, no higher
ViewModel owns the screen state; composables own ephemeral UI state (scroll position, text field focus)
Events as function parameters: onSaveClicked: () -> Unit — the composable declares what happened, the owner decides what it means
Single source of truth per state: if two composables need it, it lives above both — never duplicated and synced

example.walkthrough: The text field values are ephemeral — they live in the composable with remember. The LoginUiState lives in the ViewModel and flows down as a parameter. The login click is an event lambda flowing up. If the screen recomposes, nothing is lost; if the ViewModel updates state, the UI follows. Two tiers, one direction each.

pitfalls: Hoisting everything to the ViewModel — text field keystrokes triggering ViewModel updates is overkill
Keeping screen state in the composable — rotation wipes it; screen state belongs to the ViewModel
Side effects in composition (calling onLogin during composition) — events fire from handlers, never from the compose pass
lessons.try_it: Take one screen and label every state as ephemeral (remember) or screen state (ViewModel). Move any misplaced ones.

lessons.title: Hilt Scoping
concepts: Hilt components mirror Android lifecycles: SingletonComponent (app), ActivityRetainedComponent (ViewModel), ActivityComponent, FragmentComponent
@Singleton for app-wide singletons (repositories, Retrofit); @ViewModelScoped for per-screen instances
Scope mismatch = leak or crash: an Activity-scoped object injected into a Singleton lives forever — Hilt fails the build on scope violations
@InstallIn declares the component; qualifiers (@Named, custom) disambiguate multiple bindings of the same type
Testing: Hilt test components replace bindings — @UninstallModules plus @HiltAndroidTest for instrumented tests, constructor injection for unit tests

example.walkthrough: NetworkModule installs the API in the SingletonComponent — one instance for the app. VmModule installs the use case in the ViewModelComponent — fresh per ViewModel. Hilt's best feature is the compile-time scope check: injecting an Activity context into a Singleton is a guaranteed leak, and Hilt refuses to compile it instead of crashing at 2 AM.

pitfalls: Everything @Singleton by default — ViewModel-scoped state leaking across screens
Field injection in ViewModels — use constructor injection; field injection hides dependencies
Ignoring scope-violation build errors — they are leak reports, not nuisances
lessons.try_it: Annotate one module's bindings with the narrowest correct scope and verify the build still passes.

lessons.title: Modularization Strategies
concepts: Feature modules (:feature_feed) own screens; core modules (:core_data, :core_ui) own shared code — features depend on core, never on each other
API/impl split: :feature_feed_api exposes interfaces, :feature_feed_impl implements them — features communicate through APIs
Build speed: modules compile in parallel and incrementally — the main reason big apps modularize, ahead of reuse
Dependency rules enforced by structure: :app depends on features, features on core — circular dependencies become impossible
Start small: extract :core_ui (theme, components) and :core_data (repository, database) first — highest value, lowest risk

example.walkthrough: The dependency block is the architecture: feature modules see only core modules, never siblings. That one rule — enforced by Gradle, not convention — is what keeps a 50-module app navigable. Start with the two core extractions; they pay for themselves in build speed and clarity before you touch features.

pitfalls: Modularizing by layer (:data, :domain, :ui for the whole app) — recreates the monolith with slower builds; modularize by feature
Circular dependencies between modules — the build fails; that is the structure doing its job, fix the direction
Nano-modules (one class per module) — Gradle overhead per module; group by cohesive feature
lessons.try_it: Extract :core_ui from your app module: move the theme and 3 shared components, fix the dependencies.

lessons.title: Scoping a Take-Home Project
concepts: Reviewers grade working software first, then code quality, then architecture — a polished half beats a broken whole
Define the MVP slice: one happy path end-to-end (list to detail to action) before any second feature
Time-box ruthlessly: 40% core flow, 25% polish and tests, 20% README and demo, 15% buffer — the README is graded, the buffer is survival
Cut list in writing: offline mode, animations, dark theme — name what you are NOT building so scope stays honest
Match the prompt's stack hints: if they mention MVVM and Room, use MVVM and Room — deviating needs justification

example.walkthrough: The scope doc is the project plan: must/nice/cut makes trade-offs explicit before you are tired, the stack line proves you read the prompt, and the README line reserves time for the artifact reviewers actually read first. Thirty minutes here saves hours of mid-build scope panic.

pitfalls: Starting with the cool feature — the core flow must work first; demos die on broken happy paths
No README — reviewers will not guess your architecture; document setup, decisions, and trade-offs
Gold-plating one screen while the second screen does not exist — breadth of working flow beats depth of polish
lessons.try_it: Write a scope doc for a hypothetical take-home: must/nice/cut, stack, test plan, deliverables.

lessons.title: Networking with Retrofit and OkHttp
concepts: Retrofit turns HTTP APIs into Kotlin interfaces: @GET with suspend functions — the network becomes a function call
OkHttp interceptors: logging (debug only), auth header injection, retry — the cross-cutting layer
Error mapping: sealed ApiResult (Success/Error) at the repository boundary — the UI never sees HTTP codes
Moshi or kotlinx.serialization for JSON: codegen adapters avoid reflection — faster and R8-safe
Timeouts: configure connect, read, and write timeouts — do not let a hung server hang your UI forever

example.walkthrough: The interface is three lines — Retrofit generates the implementation. The repository translates the transport outcome into domain language: HTTP 401 becomes AuthError, IOException becomes NetworkError. The UI switches on ApiResult, never on status codes. That boundary is what makes the networking layer testable and the UI readable.

pitfalls: Exposing Response<T> or HttpException to the ViewModel — transport details leaking into UI logic
Logging interceptor in release builds — request bodies in logcat on user devices
No timeouts — a hung server holds a thread and the user waits forever
lessons.try_it: Add an auth interceptor that injects the bearer token and a 401 handler that triggers token refresh.

lessons.title: Compose State Hoisting in Practice
concepts: Hoist state to the lowest common owner: a search field used by one screen keeps its state; a filter shared by list and map hoists to the screen ViewModel
Stateless composables (state plus lambdas as parameters) are reusable and previewable — the design-system building blocks
State holders (plain classes) for complex screen state that is not ViewModel-worthy: form validation logic, wizard steps
rememberSaveable for UI state that must survive rotation; ViewModel for state tied to business logic
Unidirectional flow in practice: ViewModel to screen composable to stateless children; events bubble back up

example.walkthrough: SearchBar owns nothing — query flows in, changes flow out. That makes it trivially previewable (the @Preview passes fake data) and reusable anywhere. The ViewModel above it owns the real query state and the search action. When a composable is hard to preview, it is holding state it should not.

pitfalls: Stateful design-system components — every usage reinvents the state management
Hoisting to the Activity — state outlives the screen and leaks across navigation
Two sources of truth (composable state plus ViewModel state for the same field) — they desync
lessons.try_it: Convert one stateful composable to stateless (state plus lambdas) and add a @Preview.

lessons.title: Finding and Fixing Jank in Your Build
concepts: Profile your own build before submitting: the take-home will be judged on feel, and jank is felt instantly
GPU rendering bars on your screens: any bar over the green 16ms line is a frame your reviewer will notice
Common take-home jank: image loading without placeholders or resizing, heavy work in onBindViewHolder, unoptimized lists
Coil/Glide with explicit sizes: .size(200, 200) decodes to the view size — full-resolution loads in lists are the number one self-inflicted jank
Baseline Profiles for the demo path: your app's first impression (cold start plus first scroll) gets ahead-of-time compiled

example.code:
// Coil: decode to the view size, not the file size
AsyncImage(
    model = ImageRequest.Builder(LocalContext.current)
        .data(post.imageUrl)
        .size(400, 400) // decode to view size
        .crossfade(true)
        .build(),
    contentDescription = post.title,
    modifier = Modifier.size(200.dp),
)
example.walkthrough: The .size() call is the whole optimization: without it, Coil decodes the full-resolution image and the GPU scales it per frame — in a scrolling list, that is jank. With it, the bitmap matches the view. Pair with the GPU bars: scroll, count offending bars, add sizes, re-scroll, compare.

pitfalls: No placeholders — content pops in and layout jumps as images load
Full-size images in lists because Coil caches — the cache stores the decoded bitmap; decode size still matters
Profiling only on the emulator — GPU behavior differs; test scroll jank on a real low-end device
lessons.try_it: Enable GPU rendering bars, scroll your longest list, and fix the worst offender with explicit image sizes.

lessons.title: Self Code Review Checklist
concepts: Review your own diff before submitting: read it as the interviewer — every line should defend its existence
The checklist: no commented-out code, no TODOs without tickets, no debug logs, no hardcoded URLs or keys, consistent naming
Architecture check: does the data flow match your README diagram? Or did the build drift?
Test check: do the tests you claim exist actually run green? Run ./gradlew test before you zip
README check: setup steps work from a fresh clone — the reviewer will run them, and works-on-my-machine fails the review

example.walkthrough: The ritual is ordered by embarrassment cost: failing tests first (they will run them), then the release build (they will install it), then the README (they will follow it). The final diff read is the mindset shift — you are no longer the author defending, you are the reviewer deciding. Cut or justify everything questionable.

pitfalls: Submitting from a dirty working tree — uncommitted fixes the reviewer cannot see
README describing the app you planned, not the app you built — drift is normal, docs must match reality
Skipping the release-build smoke test — debug-only testing hides R8 and shrinking breakage
lessons.try_it: Run the full ritual on a sample project and fix everything it finds.

lessons.title: The 60-Second Coroutines Explanation
concepts: The elevator pitch structure: what (lightweight concurrency), why (no thread blocking, no callback hell), how (suspend plus scopes plus dispatchers) — in that order
The one analogy: coroutines are like threads but cheap — thousands for the price of a thread, and they do not block while waiting
Name the three pillars: suspend functions (pausable work), scopes (structured lifetime), dispatchers (where it runs)
End with a concrete: so a network call looks like a normal function call but never blocks the UI thread
Practice out loud with a timer — 60 seconds is shorter than you think; filler words eat the how

example.walkthrough: The script is timed and ordered: what (one sentence), why (the pain it kills), how (the three pillars, one line each), close (the money line of code). Interviewers score clarity under time pressure — the structure guarantees you land all three pillars before the timer, even nervous.

pitfalls: Starting with dispatchers — details before the mental model loses the listener
Saying it is like threads without the cheap-and-non-blocking distinction — invites threading questions you do not want
No concrete close — abstract explanations are forgettable; the one-liner sticks
lessons.try_it: Record yourself giving the 60-second explanation. Transcribe it and cut every filler word.

lessons.title: Whiteboard Patterns: Debounce, Cache, Retry
concepts: Whiteboard coding tests patterns, not syntax: narrate the approach before writing — I will debounce the input, switch to the latest query, cache results
Debounce from scratch: timestamp check or Handler.postDelayed with removeCallbacks — show you know the mechanism, not just the operator
Cache: a Map with the query as key — then discuss invalidation, which is the genuinely hard part
Retry: loop with exponential backoff and a max attempts cap — mention which exceptions retry
Narrate trade-offs as you write: in production I would use Flow.debounce; here is the manual version to show the mechanism

example.walkthrough: The whiteboard version proves you understand the mechanism (timestamps, dropping keystrokes); the one-liner proves you know the production tool. Interviewers want both — mechanism first, idiom second. The retry shows the same duality: manual backoff loop, then in production, retryWhen with exponential backoff. Always bridge from mechanism to idiom.

pitfalls: Writing the Flow one-liner only — they asked for the mechanism; show what is inside
Silent swallowing in retry — the last attempt must throw; swallowed errors are silent data loss
No narration — silent writing leaves the interviewer guessing; think out loud
lessons.try_it: Whiteboard (paper, no IDE) the debounce plus cache for a search box in under 10 minutes.

lessons.title: Answering 'Your Hardest Bug'
concepts: STAR for debugging stories: Situation (the symptom), Task (your responsibility), Action (the investigation), Result (the fix plus prevention)
Pick a bug with a real investigation arc: misleading symptoms, a wrong turn, the breakthrough — not a typo fix
Show the method: logs, profilers, bisecting, reproduction — interviewers hire debugging process, not the specific bug
The wrong turn is the best part: assuming it was the network for a day shows honest reasoning and course correction
Close with prevention: the test, the monitor, or the checklist that stops it recurring — seniors prevent, juniors fix

example.walkthrough: The outline forces the right proportions: most candidates spend 80% on the Situation and mumble the Action. Flip it — the investigation is the interview. Name the tools (GPU bars, profiler), the wrong turn (assumed debug equals release), the breakthrough (R8 plus image size). The prevention close is what separates senior answers from junior ones.

pitfalls: Blaming others in the story — interviewers hear how you will talk about them
A bug with no investigation (I googled the error) — pick one where you actually reasoned
No prevention close — the story ends at the fix instead of the lesson
lessons.try_it: Write your hardest-bug STAR outline (5 bullet points) and time yourself telling it in 3 minutes.

lessons.title: System Design: The Feed
concepts: Scope first: a read-heavy feed with images, pull-to-refresh, offline support — ask the scale before designing
The layers: UI (Compose plus ViewModel plus paging), data (repository, Room cache, Retrofit), sync (WorkManager)
Paging 3: the expected answer for infinite lists — PagingSource, RemoteMediator for network plus database
Image strategy: Coil with size-matched requests, disk cache, placeholders — the performance story
Offline: Room as source of truth, RemoteMediator refresh, sync status — tie back to the offline-first lessons

example.walkthrough: Draw the boxes before explaining — interviewers follow diagrams better than monologues. The three sentences to land: UI never touches the network, Room is the source of truth, RemoteMediator bridges network and database. Every follow-up (offline? images? scale?) maps to one box, which is why the diagram carries the answer.

pitfalls: Jumping to code — design the boxes first, code only if asked
No offline story — mobile system design without offline is incomplete
Forgetting the image story — feeds are image-heavy; sizing and caching are expected
lessons.try_it: Draw the feed architecture from memory in 5 minutes, then narrate it in 2.

lessons.title: Full-Loop Interview Simulation Prep
concepts: The full loop: coding plus system design plus behavioral in one day — energy management matters as much as knowledge
Before: sleep, the 60-second pitches (coroutines, hardest bug, your project), whiteboard patterns rehearsed — no new material the night before
During: narrate constantly, ask clarifying questions before coding, manage the clock (state your plan: 10 min design, 20 min code, 10 min tests)
Between rounds: reset — water, notes on what worked, no spiraling on the last round
After: same-day thank-you notes referencing specific discussion points — the loop is not over when you leave

example.walkthrough: The timeline treats the interview as a performance with a taper: heavy prep ends 3 days out, the day before is rest, loop day is execution. The in-room tactics — narrating, clarifying first, time-boxing aloud — are what interviewers actually score. The retro closes the loop so each interview makes the next one better.

pitfalls: Cramming new topics the night before — low retention, high anxiety; review, do not learn
Silent problem-solving — the interviewer cannot score what they cannot hear
No questions for them — asking what success looks like in 90 days shows you think like an owner
lessons.try_it: Do a full 45-minute mock round with a friend: 10 min design, 25 min code, 10 min Q&A. Retro after.

simulations.title: The ANR in the final round
simulations.brief: Play Console flags your checkout flow: the ANR rate spiked to 2.1% after the last release. Walk the interviewer through your diagnosis.

steps.symptom: ANR traces show the main thread blocked for 5.2 seconds inside CheckoutRepository.sync() during a network call.
evidence:
main tid=1 blocked 5.2s
  at CheckoutRepository.sync (CheckoutRepository.kt:41)
  at CheckoutViewModel.onPay (CheckoutViewModel.kt:88)
ANR rate 2.1% (bad-behavior threshold 0.47%), clustered on the checkout screen
options: Move the network call off the main thread with viewModelScope.launch(Dispatchers.IO)
Add StrictMode penalties so the ANR logs more detail
Raise the ANR timeout in the manifest
Show a loading spinner while the main thread finishes
steps.explain: The main thread must never do network I/O. Moving the call to Dispatchers.IO inside viewModelScope fixes the root cause; the other options hide or decorate the freeze.

steps.symptom: The freeze is gone, but rotating the phone during checkout now crashes: IllegalStateException, view already detached.
evidence:
java.lang.IllegalStateException: Fragment CheckoutFragment not attached
  at CheckoutRepository$sync$2.invokeSuspend (launched in GlobalScope)
options: Scope the coroutine to the UI lifecycle with viewModelScope or lifecycleScope instead of GlobalScope
Catch IllegalStateException around every UI call
Disable rotation in the manifest
Move the network call back to the main thread
steps.explain: GlobalScope outlives the screen. viewModelScope cancels automatically when the ViewModel clears, so detached-view crashes disappear by construction.

steps.symptom: Fix verified on device. The interviewer asks: how do you prove this stays fixed in CI?
evidence: ./gradlew connectedCheck runs on every PR — no coroutine tests exist yet
options: Add a test on a TestDispatcher asserting the repository never touches the main thread, and gate merges on it
Rely on manual QA rotation tests before each release
Test only on a Pixel with developer options on
Delete the UI test module to keep CI fast
steps.explain: A regression test on a test dispatcher makes the fix structural: any future main-thread I/O fails the build instead of reaching users.

simulations.debrief: ANRs are a main-thread discipline problem: I/O leaves the main thread, coroutines die with their scope, and a dispatcher test locks the fix in CI.

simulations.title: The leaking Activity
simulations.brief: LeakCanary fires after every rotation of the settings screen. The interviewer wants the leak found, fixed, and proven gone.

steps.symptom: LeakCanary: SettingsActivity leaked — one retained instance after rotation, 12 MB held.
evidence:
SettingsActivity leaked via
  static Analytics.tracker → Context field
  (tracker holds the Activity instance)
options: Break the static reference: pass applicationContext to the tracker, or hold a WeakReference
Call System.gc() in onDestroy
Set largeHeap=true in the manifest
Ignore it — 12 MB is small
steps.explain: A static field is a GC root: anything it touches lives forever. applicationContext is process-scoped and safe to hold; the Activity is not.

steps.symptom: Static reference fixed. Now the location callback keeps the map screen alive after the user navigates away.
evidence:
locationClient.requestUpdates(callback) // never removed
// callback is an inner class of MapActivity
options: Unregister the callback in onStop/onDestroy — every register needs a matching unregister
Make the callback static and keep it registered
Post the unregister to a Handler with a delay
Move registration to Application.onCreate
steps.explain: Listeners are the classic second leak: registration without unregistration pins the host. Pair every register with an unregister in the matching lifecycle callback.

steps.symptom: Both leaks fixed. How do you prove it to the interviewer?
evidence: Rotate the device 10 times on the settings and map screens
options: Rotate repeatedly and confirm LeakCanary reports zero retained instances
Check the APK size shrank
Profile once and eyeball the heap graph
Ship and watch crash-free sessions
steps.explain: The proof is mechanical: rotate, and LeakCanary stays silent. Leak detection is a regression gate, not a one-time cleanup.

simulations.debrief: Leaks are lifetime mismatches: statics and listeners that outlive their Activity. Fix the reference, pair register with unregister, and let LeakCanary guard the fix.

simulations.title: The flaky UI test
simulations.brief: Your Espresso checkout test passes locally and fails on CI every third run. The loop interviewer asks you to stabilize it live.

steps.symptom: The test taps Pay then asserts the receipt screen; on CI the receipt sometimes has not loaded when the assertion runs.
options: Synchronize with the app's async work — register an IdlingResource or drive the test with a TestDispatcher
Add Thread.sleep(3000) before the assertion
Run the test 5 times and take the majority result
Mark the test @Ignore on CI
steps.explain: Flakiness is unsynchronized async work. Idling resources make Espresso wait for the real condition; sleeps just move the race and slow the suite.

steps.symptom: IdlingResource added. The test still flakes when the fake payment gateway responds slowly.
evidence: val gateway = RealGateway(sandboxUrl) // hits network in tests
options: Replace the gateway with a fake that returns instantly and deterministically
Increase the Espresso idling timeout to 60s
Retry the whole test class on failure
Run UI tests only on release branches
steps.explain: UI tests must not touch the network. A fake gateway removes the last nondeterminism; the network boundary belongs in a separate integration test.

steps.symptom: Green 20/20. The interviewer asks how this stays green.
options: Keep the test in the PR gate and treat any new flake as a blocking bug, not a retry
Quarantine it in a nightly job nobody watches
Allow 2 retries in the CI config
Delete it now that the feature shipped
steps.explain: A flaky-test culture starts with one tolerated retry. Gating on it and treating flakes as bugs keeps the suite trustworthy.

simulations.debrief: Flaky UI tests are synchronization bugs: wait on real conditions, fake the network, and gate on the result.

simulations.title: The Room migration crash
simulations.brief: Release 2.4 adds a column to the articles table. Users updating from 2.3 crash on launch. Diagnose it like a senior would.

steps.symptom: Crash on launch for upgraders only: IllegalStateException, a migration from 1 to 2 was required but not found.
evidence: Room cannot verify the data integrity — migration 1 -> 2 missing
options: Supply Migration(1, 2) with the ALTER TABLE that adds the column
Set fallbackToDestructiveMigration() and ship
Tell users to reinstall
Bump to version 3 and hope Room figures it out
steps.explain: Room requires an explicit migration path. Destructive fallback deletes user data — the one thing an upgrade must never do.

steps.symptom: Migration written. How do you test it before it reaches users?
evidence: androidx.room:room-testing is already in the project
options: Use MigrationTestHelper: create v1, insert rows, run the migration, assert the data survives
Install the release APK over the debug APK manually once
Trust the ALTER TABLE syntax
Test only fresh installs
steps.explain: MigrationTestHelper automates the upgrade path: old schema, real data, then the migration. Manual once-testing does not survive the next schema change.

steps.symptom: Migration tested. The interviewer asks about a column rename instead of an add.
options: Write Migration(2, 3) that creates the new table, copies data, drops the old, renames — SQLite has no RENAME COLUMN on older APIs
Use ALTER TABLE RENAME COLUMN and require API 30+
Destructive migration for renames only
Skip the version bump for renames
steps.explain: Room supports renames via the table-copy pattern. On older SQLite there is no rename primitive, so the migration does it in four explicit steps.

simulations.debrief: Schema changes are contracts with existing user data: explicit migrations, MigrationTestHelper proof, and never destructive fallback on a real database.

simulations.title: Whiteboard: offline-first feed
simulations.brief: System-design round: design an offline-first news feed in 40 minutes. Talk through tradeoffs, not just the happy path.

steps.symptom: Requirements: the feed must render instantly offline, refresh when online, and survive process death.
options: Single source of truth: a Room cache serves the UI via Flow; network refresh writes into Room
The UI reads the network directly and caches in memory
Two sources: the UI merges network and cache responses itself
SharedPreferences for the article list
steps.explain: One source of truth keeps the UI simple: it always renders the cache, and refresh is a cache write. Merging in the UI duplicates consistency logic everywhere.

steps.symptom: The interviewer pushes: what happens when the refresh fails halfway through?
evidence: 500 articles written, then the connection drops
options: Write the refresh in a Room transaction — partial writes roll back, the cache stays consistent
Leave the partial page; the next refresh fixes it
Clear the cache on any failure
Show an error and require pull-to-refresh
steps.explain: Transactions make refresh atomic: users never see a half-written page. Consistency is a database property, not a UI prayer.

steps.symptom: Last 10 minutes: how does the UI stay responsive while the refresh runs?
evidence: Compose screen collecting the feed Flow
options: The repository exposes Flow from Room on Dispatchers.IO; the UI collects with lifecycle awareness — no main-thread I/O anywhere
Refresh on the main thread but show a spinner
Poll the database on a timer from the Activity
Load everything into memory at startup
steps.explain: Room + Flow already moves work off the main thread; lifecycle-aware collection cancels when the screen goes away. Responsiveness is architecture, not spinners.

simulations.debrief: Offline-first is one decision repeated everywhere: the database is the source of truth, refreshes are atomic writes, and the UI only ever reads the cache.

cheatsheet: Null safety: `?.` safe call, `?:` Elvis, `let` scoping; `!!` is a scheduled NPE; `lateinit`/`by lazy` for deferred init.
Data class: equals/hashCode/toString/copy/destructuring. Sealed: restricted hierarchy + exhaustive when.
Extensions resolve statically — no overriding, no privates, no state. Delegation (`by`) generates forwarding.
Lifecycle: onCreate -> onStart -> onResume; onPause -> onStop -> onDestroy. onPause must be fast.
Survival buckets: ViewModel (rotation), onSaveInstanceState (process death), DB/files (permanent).
Coroutines: suspend pauses without blocking; scope owns lifetime; Dispatchers: Main/Default/IO; cancellation is cooperative.
Flows: StateFlow = state (has value, conflates); SharedFlow = events (replay configurable); catch keeps flows alive.
Operators: debounce, distinctUntilChanged, flatMapLatest (cancels stale), flowOn, stateIn(WhileSubscribed).
Persistence: DataStore (prefs) < Room (queryable) < Keystore/EncryptedPrefs (secrets); images on disk, not in DB.
Architecture: UiState in StateFlow; events up via sealed interface; repository owns data policy; Hilt scopes match lifetimes.
glossary: ANR
Application Not Responding: main thread blocked ~5s on input; diagnosed from main-thread traces.
Dispatcher
Coroutine thread pool: Main (UI), Default (CPU), IO (blocking I/O).
Exhaustive when
Compiler-enforced branch coverage over sealed hierarchies.
FlatMapLatest
Flow operator switching to the newest upstream, cancelling the previous.
Sealed interface
Restricted type hierarchy enabling exhaustive when.
StateFlow
Hot observable state holder: always has a value, conflates updates.
Structured concurrency
Child coroutines bound to a parent scope's lifetime and failure policy.
UDF
Unidirectional data flow: events up, state down, single reduction point.
ViewModel
Lifecycle-aware state holder surviving configuration changes.
Tombstone
Delete marker synced so offline deletes propagate instead of resurrecting.
checklist: Can you explain suspend vs blocking and pick the right dispatcher for any job?
Can you narrate the activity lifecycle and place every state in its survival bucket?
Can you build the search-as-you-type Flow pipeline from memory and justify each operator?
Do you have two STAR stories rehearsed under 3 minutes?
Have you done one timed mock per loop type (coding, architecture, debugging, behavioral)?
Does your take-home survive rotation, airplane mode, and 'Don't keep activities'?
